subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time that I adjourned the debate yesterday I was criticizing the federal government policy that apparently has influenced the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to advise farmers to reduce their production of livestock. I had called such a policy an anti-social one and had suggested that it might have an adverse effect upon the agricultural program in western Canada. I call it an anti-social program because I consider it to be a retrograde step back to the policies of the 1930's. It is apparently an attempt to bolster prices by creating a scarcity for fear that we might have an artificial surplus. I use the word "artificial" because no one can argue that there is an actual surplus of livestock products in the world today. In many parts of the world meat is still being rationed. Furthermore, I think it makes a mockery of the declaration of principles of the United Nations Organization to which we have subscribed and to which we have pledged ourselves to do everything possible to eliminate want in the world. I also recall that the Minister of Agriculture, when speaking to the food and agriculture organization conference some years ago, expressed himself to the effect that never again would the people of the world tolerate a situation where food was destroyed while there were hungry people. Of course when you reduce production you are destroying a potential supply.
On the second point, that it might interfere with the agricultural program in western Canada, I recall that for many years hon.

members from eastern Canada were most critical in the house of the farmers of western Canada for depending upon one crop. The cry we used to hear in the year 1935 and onward was that the farmers of the west should diversify, that they should raise more livestock. In recent years the farmers of the west have diversified. They have gone into livestock extensively. They have gone into crop rotation, and it was very wise that they did because by growing more grasses and keeping more pasture land they have helped to restore fibre in the soil and thereby prevent soil drifting. But the farmers of the west are now being advised to cut down their livestock. Once again the pasture land may be plowed up and once again there will be the danger of soil drifting.
The Minister of Agriculture argued in his speech in the house that the best market was the home market. I think we all agree with him that the best market is undoubtedly the home market. That is why we in this group have time and again urged the government to maintain the purchasing power of the people at all times at a level that will make it possible for them to buy the production of the country and the imports that can be brought into the country in exchange for our exports. But on the other hand, of course, there are many commodities that we can produce in excess of home needs, and so we export this surplus to bring imports into the country.
With a few exceptions, a very large percentage of our farm products is consumed within the domestic market. Unfortunately the small percentage exported abroad dominates to a great extent the prices received for the goods sold in the home market. I would point out that has not been the case with regard to the secondary industries. In so far as they are concerned, they have made a practice of selling in the domestic market at the best price they can get, at a price which returns to them a fair profit, and then they have exported their surplus and sold it at whatever price it would bring on the world market. In other words, the secondary industries have followed the practice of adopting a two-price system for their production.
From time to time we have urged the adoption of a similar policy so far as agriculture is concerned. Of recent years western farm organizations have urged the adoption of a two-price system for the sale of agricultural products, especially with respect to the sale of wheat. They have urged that wheat sold in the domestic market should be sold at a parity price, and then

wheat exported would be sold at the price under the international wheat agreement or as class II wheat.
There would of course be greater difficulty in applying a two-price system to the marketing of livestock products than would be the case with wheat because as far as wheat is concerned it is handled under the wheat board. However, we in this group believe that it would be to the advantage of agriculture and the whole Canadian economy if a national livestock marketing board were set up which would have full control over the marketing and purchasing of farm products. First of all we think that a plebiscite should be held to find out whether or not the farmers would support such a program, in the same way that a plebiscite was taken in Manitoba as to the sale of oats and barley through the wheat board. If the farmers voted in favour of it, then of course it would require enabling legislation by the provinces. In that way there would be no difficulty in having a two-price system. Farm products consumed in Canada would be sold at parity prices and farm products exported would be sold at the best price that could be obtained in the international market. An initial payment would be made when the products were purchased, and the final payment would be made at the end of the year, balancing the price obtained from goods sold in the domestic and external markets.
I am quite well aware of the fact that some people will brand such a policy as a form of protection, but as long as the farmers of Canada have to pay a protected price for practically everything they buy then I say they are entitled to protected prices for those things that they sell. When I say "protected", I do not merely mean protected by tariff because there are many forms of protection in this country. There is the tariff. There is the question of minimum wage laws and wage agreements which, of course, have an effect on prices. There is the question of railway tariffs which afford the railways protection against competition. There are the social security programs which are a protection affecting prices, and of course there are support prices. These various forms of protection all have an effect upon the prices at which commodities are sold. Therefore, I say that so long as farmers have to pay those protective prices they are entitled to protective prices for the things they sell.
As I pointed out yesterday, I am not surprised and I am not criticizing the Minister of Agriculture for having advised farmers in 68108-185
The Budget-Mr. Quelch conference in Victoria to reduce their production of livestock in order to get better prices. No doubt he thinks that is the wise thing to do in the light of the existing international situation. However, I think it is high time we adopted international trade policies that would fit the needs of the various nations rather than trying to mould the economies of those various nations to fit into the pattern of some international trade agreement such as the Bretton Woods agreement.
ft is quite obvious by this time that the Bretton Woods agreement, especially the international monetary fund, and the Geneva trade agreements have not been a success in achieving a balance of international payments and thereby paving the way for convertibility.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in delivering his budget had this to say at page 2117 of Hansard:
The major instruments for international economic co-operation which were drawn up immediately after the war, namely the Bretton Woods agreement and the general agreement on tariffs and trade, envisaged that convertibility of currencies and multilateral trade would have been restored over a larger part of the world by now.
A little further on he said:
It is clear that the time has come for new initiatives.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we hope that the new initiatives will be exercised in the right direction because they might even make the situation worse if pursued in the wrong direction. It is hoped that we now fully realize the fundamental weaknesses of the Bretton Woods agreement, especially in regard to the international monetary fund.
At the time the Bretton Woods agreement was debated in the house in 1945, we in this group stressed the need for recognition of the fact that balancing international trade was the joint responsibility of both the creditor and the debtor nations. We attacked the Bretton Woods agreement as having a very definite pro creditor bias. We pointed out that debtor nations were only able to balance their payments if the creditor nations were willing to accept goods in payment for their exports. The Bretton Woods agreement places great pressure on the debtor nations but applies little or no pressure on the creditor nations.
It is interesting to note in that regard that the United States are the main culprits. When the Bretton Woods agreement was before the banking and commerce committee in 1945 I had stressed that point and I pointed out that on the record of the past there was little reason to expect that the United States would act as a good creditor under the international monetary fund, and

The Budget-Mr. Quelch that unless they did change their policy there was little or no chance of success within that agreement.
Here is a reply made by Mr. Rasminsky on page 29 of the proceedings:
You say that the United States on her past record can be counted upon to act as a bad creditor. I would reply to that that on the basis of the experience before the war there is reason for misgiving regarding the willingness or the ability of the United States to carry out the type of economic policy appropriate to her creditor position.
Then he goes on to point out that certain trade proposals had been put forward by the United States which gave him reason to hope that the United States would change their policies in the future. Later on I stressed the responsibility of the creditor nations to accept payment in goods, and Mr. Rasminsky had this to say in reply, on page 59 of the proceedings:
Yes. The only answer that one can give to your question is that in the final analysis, that debt can only be discharged through the movement of goods, t am assuming now that the debtor country has not any independent monetary reserves of its own; and there is the question that Mr. Quelch has insisted on, of the responsibility of the creditor to facilitate the movement of goods that will enable the debtor to discharge his debt. I have indicated today, I think-and at some length last night-that I agree with Mr. Quelch that in the final analysis the creditor country must pursue policies that will enable the debtor to discharge its indebtedness.
In spite of that we went ahead with the Bretton Woods agreement trusting that the United States was going to change her policy in that regard and, as a creditor nation in the future, be willing to allow debtor nations to pay their debts in goods. What has been the situation? Was that hope of Mr. Rasminsky justified? It is now seven years since that agreement was signed. It is interesting to read what the governor of the Bank of Canada had to say in his report for 1952 as found on page 11 thereof:
More than seven years have now passed since the end of the war and it must be acknowledged that the world is still far from the goals of currency convertibility and non-discrimination; indeed, restrictions on trade and payments are in many cases more rather than less severe than they were some years ago.
On page 12 he says:
If it is the primary responsibility of the deficit countries so to conduct their affairs that there is available for export a sufficient quantity of goods at competitive prices, so is it the primary responsibility of the surplus countries to allow competition from abroad to take place, and not to prevent but rather to encourage an increased inflow of goods. There is no need to underline the importance in this connection of the policies pursued by the United States.
Further down:
The difficulties involved in the deficit countries achieving balance through an increase in "hard currency" exports rather than by continuing to
tMr. Quelch.]

rely heavily on import restrictions and discrimination may well appear to them insuperable if United States actions limit severely their chances of earning dollars by competing in the American market. Restrictions in the United States cannot fail to encourage restrictions elsewhere.
Now, seven years after the passing of the Bretton Woods agreement, when Mr. Rasminsky stated that there was every reason to believe that the United States were going to change their policy, we have the governor of the Bank of Canada regretting that the United States is not making it possible for debtor nations to pay for their goods by the acceptance of their exports. I would say that if a new initiative is to be used to seek solutions, we should place the responsibility equitably upon both debtor and creditor nations, and not just depend upon a change of attitude by the United States for the success of the agreement. By that I mean that if we realize that in order to achieve a balance of international payments it is essential that a creditor nation shall accept payment in goods, we must place that obligation in writing in the agreement rather than depend upon a change of policy on the part of creditor nations that have not been adopting that policy in the past. Because, mind you, while we just depended on hope that the United States would change their policy under the Bretton Woods agreement, we did not depend on hope as far as the debtor nations were concerned. We placed a definite responsibility upon the debtor nations to balance their payments. If they fail to do so they may be penalized by an increase in the interest rate. As I say, we have placed a penalty upon the debtor nations but not upon the creditor nations.
As Mr. Towers says, it is a joint responsibility. Therefore, in the future, if we are going to make any changes or institute any new international agreements, let us provide that the creditor nation will have to accept a share of responsibility along with the debtor nation. Under the Bretton Woods agreement a creditor nation has the right to demand payment in its own currency.
Now, what is the real purpose of international trade? The real purpose of international trade is the exchange of goods and services on the basis of mutual advantage. Therefore, if nations are sincere in subscribing to that type of policy, then all the creditor nation needs is to accept the currency of the importing nation rather than demanding its own currency, because with the currency of the importing nation it will be in a position to buy anything that nation produces. If it is sincere in saying it is going to balance its trade, the only type of

currency it needs is the currency of the importing nation, rather than demanding its own currency.
I should like to quote from a summary I made in 1945 dealing with the situation. I shall quote briefly from it, because I think it applies today just as much as it applied then. On page 131 of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee for 1945 I stated:
What we want in the act mainly is a provision that a debtor nation in order to pay for its imports shall be recognized as paying for them when they establish a credit within their country in favour of a creditor nation and that that credit can be used to buy anything purchased within that country. Then if the creditor nation is not willing to accept goods from a nation with which it has a credit if it desires to trade on a multilateral basis it may trade the credit established on that basis for the credit of another country on a multilateral basis. So I say if the great industrialized nations are really sincere in this matter they should have shown it at this time and been willing to have an article to that effect put in the Bretton Woods agreement.
Had that been done, we would not today have a situation where the governor of the Bank of Canada is deploring the fact that the United States is still the main culprit in refusing to accept imports in payment for their exports as they did prior to the time the Bretton Woods agreement was passed. Under such a policy trade with the sterling area could be expanded and production within the sterling area could be expanded. It would, in that way, provide greater markets for Canada's agricultural products. There would be no need to reduce production of livestock as suggested by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Provided we adopted the two-price system we would be able to obtain a fair price, an average between the domestic price and parity with world market prices. I believe that today is an opportune time to press for changes in the Bretton Woods agreement, because at last there does seem to be greater realization on the part of the people of the United States of the responsibility they have to make it possible for other nations to balance their payments with them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the week of February 28, Mr. H. R. Anderson, who I understand is vice-president and general manager of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, made a speech to the North Burnaby board of trade, and the keynote of that speech was that Burnaby and the lower mainland of British Columbia generally would benefit, in many ways, as the result of the building of the pipe line from the Alberta oil fields to British Columbia, and with that idea I 68108-1851	.
The Budget-Mr. Goode have no argument. He went on to say that it would take 2J million gallons of oil to keep the pipe line full and that this oil content would have a value of some $6| million. He gave a long story on the additional pumping station needed on the route and he talked about the cost of the large tanx farm being built for oil storage on Burnaby mountain.
Then the speaker, Mr. Anderson, as reported in the Burnaby Advertiser of February 26, blasted British Columbia members of parliament for being opposed to the Sumas cut-off, saying that before tankers could be used on Burrard inlet much work would have to be done on the entrance to Vancouver harbour.
I had no intention of making a speech on the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company or anything else at this time, but I consider that the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia are being hoodwinked by Mr. Anderson, and I wish to bring to the attention of the House of Commons what has happened in regard to the so-called all-Canada pipe line of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. First may I say that any objections Mr. Anderson may have to the condition of the entrance to the Vancouver harbour were taken care of in the speech from the throne at the present session when the government submitted its intention of spending large sums of money to deepen the entrance, and Mr. Anderson knew that when he made his speech in North Burnaby.
I want to refer back to the committee meetings of the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee of March 19, 1951, when the members of that committee gave full investigation to an application for the charter of Trans Mountain, and I wish to bring to your attention certain statements made by the officials of the Trans Mountain company to the committee. When 1 am finished I believe that this house and the people of Canada may have occasion to request that this charter be reinvestigated. On March 19, 1951, Mr. S. M. Blair, who was introduced to the committee as the parliamentary agent for the company, was questioned by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite). On page 88 of the proceedings, the hon. member for Skeena submitted the following question:
Will this Trans Mountain company be in the business of buying and selling oil or just carrying oil for other people?
Mr. Blair answered:
Its primary purpose is to carry oil.

The Budget-Mr. Goode
Further down the page the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Robinson) asked a series of questions as follows:
Q. I understand your present intention is that the line shall end at Vancouver.
A. That is correct.
Q. Are you at the present time considering any plans for an extension of the line from Vancouver to Portland or Seattle or other places.
A. No, it is our intention to go to a terminal at Vancouver.
Q. You have no plans and you have not considered taking the line further south in the states?
A. No, our present plans are entirely with respect to the bulk terminal at Vancouver, other arrangements being in the future.
Q. You will find the necessary refinery capacity at Vancouver?
A. That, you appreciate, will be the responsibility or the undertaking of the different refining companies. There will undoubtedly be refinery expansion concurrent with pipe line construction, but what the refinery companies' plans are I am not in a position to say.
This question, Mr. Speaker, is in connection with the amendment to be proposed by a C.C.F. member of the committee.
Mr. Robinson-
Q. Mr. Blair, are you familiar with the wording of the amendment which Mr. Herridge mentioned.
A. Yes, I am familiar with the wording as it was stated in the other hearing.
I will mention the amendment further on in my argument.
I continue quoting:
Q. And it is that wording you say you will welcome with open arms.
A. We welcome it for the reason that it in no way conflicts with our intention. Our intention is to build the line from Edmonton to Vancouver with the terminal there. The pipe line will be entirely in Canada and we will finish it in that manner.
Q. I would just like to get your idea of the effect of the amendment should your intention change in future. Should your intentions in the future come to be along the lines that you would like to extend your pipe line into the States, do you think or would you consider that you would be bound by that amendment and that you could not do so.
A. I would understand that amendment, sir, as meaning that we are confining our operations to Canada. We do not visualize any pipe line outside of our own country.
Q. Let me put it this way. Suppose you want to go into the United States, do you think that you would have to come back to parliament and ask to have other powers. I just want to get your idea on how far the amendment would bind you.
A. I do not know that I am in a position to answer that legal question. We are just not planning that sort of development.
Now I wish to put on the record, Mr. Speaker, paragraph (a) of section 6 of Bill No. 115, which concerns the charter of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, and which was not only passed by the committee but was approved by this house. Paragraph
(a)	as amended, reads as follows:
Within or outside Canada construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold, develop,


operate, maintain, control, lease mortgage created liens upon, sell, convey or otherwise dispose of and turn to account any and all interprovincial and/or international pipe lines-
And this is the amendment:
-provided that the main pipe line or lines for the transmission or transportation of oil shall be located entirely within Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the paragraph goes on with technical terms to its completion, but the essence of the intention of the committee and of the house is contained in the part of the paragraph that I have placed on the record. I now wish to continue with evidence given at the committee hearings, and I quote again questions asked by the members and answers given thereto. The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Robinson), as reported on page 92 of the committee record, at this time addressing Mr. R. L. Bridges, director of the Bechtel Corporation, asked:
Q. I have an additional question, Mr. Chairman. What do you contemplate doing with the excess, with the amount over the 30,000 barrels out of your prospective 70,000 barrels per day, which would be the capacity of your pipe line?
A. I think it would be exported.
On page 93 of the proceedings the hon. member for Simcoe East resumed his questioning:
Q. Mr. Bridges, I presume the excess would be exported; how would it be exported, by barge?
A. By tanker or barge.
Q. From what contemplated place?
A. You understand, it would be the oil companies doing this. We merely deliver the oil at the terminal, but we would assume that it would be going down into the States.
Q. And by tanker?
A. By tanker and barge.
Q. Not by an extension of your line?
A. Not in so far as the pipe line company is concerned.
On page 94 of the proceedings a question by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray), still speaking to Mr. Bridges:
Q. Would this witness say whether he would serve the Canadian navy at Vancouver or the United States navy or the British navy?
A. We would furnish anyone who had need for crude oil there.
Meaning Vancouver.
Actually we would not own the oil, but we would do servicing within the capacity of the marine terminal.
Q. Well, if the Middle East were tied up as a source of oil they would naturally turn to your supplies at Vancouver?
A. That is correct.
I wish to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that Mr. Bridges definitely stated in the committee hearings that all the oil carried in the pipe line outside of that used for domestic consumption in British Columbia was to be shipped by tanker and barge to export markets, and I wish to tell the house at this moment, to be absolutely

fair, that a large tank farm is being established on Burnaby mountain in the constituency of Burnaby-Richmond in British Columbia, and that there is considerable construction either being proceeded with or contemplated on the waterfront to assist the refiners in some export business.
But at this time I also wish to bring to the attention of the house the fact that not only did the committee understand that all oil carried through this pipe line was to find its eventual destination on the Burnaby waterfront, but that this bill was passed by the house on March 20, 1951, as reported on page 1459 of Hansard of that year, with the amendment attached thereto. The amendment was read by the chairman of the committee in response to a question asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), and there can be no doubt in any hon. member's mind that it was the intention of this house to pass a bill establishing an allCanadian pipe line, with all the oil going to the Burnaby tank farm and either being used for British Columbia consumption or to be exported via Burrard inlet to outside markets.
On February 6, 1953, the board of transport commissioners in Ottawa heard an application, under sections 11 and 12 and other sections of the Pipe Lines Act, for an order granting the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company leave to construct a pipe line- and listen to this-consisting of one or more lines of pipe for the transportation of oil from a point in section 28, township 19, east of the coast meridian in the province of British Columbia, thence in a southwesterly direction for approximately 5 [DOT] 5 miles to a point on the international border between Canada and the United States of America in section 6, township 19, east of the coast meridian. What these technical terms actually mean is that a cut-off located in Sumas in the Fraser valley is to be constructed south to the international border for the purpose of carrying oil to the United States. For the information of hon. members not familiar with that part of the country, this point is approximately fifty miles east of Burnaby.
During the hearing of the application the following gentlemen were present to support the application: Mr. H. E. B. Coyne, Q.C., for the applicant; Mr. J. J. Frawlev, Q.C., representing the attorney general of the province of Alberta; and an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Suffice it to say that the application was granted. And now the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company have permission, as far as the board of transport commissioners are concerned, to construct one or more lines of pipe carrying oil to the
The Budget-Mr. Goode United States before that oil arrives at the terminal in Burnaby. I submit to hon. members that this was not the intention of the House of Commons when it passed Bill No. 115, and that the people of British Columbia and Canada have been double-crossed by the action of the pipe line company.
I should like to refer for a moment to some of the statements made at the hearing. The same Mr. S. M. Blair, who still is the vicepresident of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, was questioned by Mr. Coyne, and as reported on page 3087 of the proceedings this question was asked:
Q. I suppose there is no proposal or thought, at this time anyway, of constructing another line from your western terminus down into the States too, is there?
A. No, this would be it. This line would feed any future refineries going in there.
Q. This, as far as you know, will be the only branch from the main line?
A. Yes.
And may I refer to a question asked by the assistant chief of the board of transport commissioners when he queried Mr. Blair on the size of this five-mile pipe line. The answer given was that it was a 24-inch line, the same size as the main line.
Mr. Blair also placed on the record that the local market in British Columbia is now in the order of a 50,000 barrel market per day and that a general shortage of oil on the whole Pacific seaboard has occurred and that imports of 140,000 barrels per day are required to supplement California production and satisfy the demands of United States west coast refineries. Mr. Blair also went on to say that the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company plans to instal a third pump station in connection with this new line which will increase the capacity of the line to the United States to 120,000 barrels per day, and he implied that this oil would go down to a refinery at present being constructed at Fern-dale, in the state of Washington. It is expected that the refinery will be completed in 1954.
At this juncture I would suggest to hon. members that they obtain a copy of the evidence given by this company on February 6, because it will be an education to them, not only in regard to the construction of pipe lines, but a lesson in the way that companies can circumvent the intention of the House of Commons. There is no doubt in my mind that the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company had no intention of telling the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines their final intention. They agreed to the amendment wholeheartedly, and knew that some time in the future they would not only

291$
The Budget-Mr. Goode double-cross the people of British Columbia, but laugh at a verdict arrived at by the members of this house.
I do not wish to comment on the matter further. X have placed the essential facts before the house for any action that they may deem necessary, but there is one matter that I would like to mention at this time, a matter so serious to the people of my riding that it is necessary for me to speak of it now. As reported on page 3084 of the evidence, an affidavit was read signed by Mr. Sherwood Lett of 626 West Pender street, in the city of Vancouver, which reads as follows:
1.	I have searched the editions of the Vancouver Daily Province and the Vancouver Sun, published on the 13th, 14th, 15th and 16th days of January, 1953, and find that on each of the said dates a notice was published, true copies of which are attached hereto.
These notices gave the intention of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company to apply to the board of transport commissioners.
2.	That the said notice was published in four consecutive issues of each of the papers aforesaid.
These notices were published at the direction of the board, stating the oil company's intention to apply for the judgment given to them on February 6, 1953.
Another letter from Mr. Sherwood Lett was put in as evidence which read as follows- the letter is addressed to a Mr. Wahn who, I understand, is secretary of the pipe line company:
Dear Mr. Wahn:
Confirming our long distance telephone conversation today, as requested I spoke to the Hon. R. W. Bonner, Q.C., Attorney General of the province of British Columbia, and referred him to the notice which had been served upon him in connection with the above matter and the hearing before the Board of Transport Commissioners on February 6. Mr. Bonner informed me that the province of British Columbia is not going to appear at the hearing, and accordingly it followed that he was not going to object to the application. Mr. Bonner stated that he had received Mr. Bridges' letter and had referred it to Mr. McLean of his department If a reply has not been sent he will see that the letter is replied to.
And this is the reply from Mr. Bonner to Mr. Bridges:
Dear Mr. Bridges:
Your letter of January 14 is hereby acknowledged. Following receipt of your letter, we have studied the matter of the application which your company proposes to make in connection with your branch line extension from the vicinity of Sumas to the international boundary. Under the circumstances, we feel that the province need not be represented at the hearing.
On page 3079 of the evidence the assistant chief of the board of transport commissioners, evidently concerned over the non-appearance of the government of British Columbia, asked

the question: "Anyone here appearing on behalf of the province of British Columbia?" And there was no answer.
I have quoted, Mr. Speaker, the evidence given before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and I have offered to you the subsequent actions of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, proving, I think, that they had no intention of carrying out the orders of this House of Commons. I have also placed on the record the refusal of the attorney general of the province of British Columbia to appear at the hearing, even though the province of Alberta considered it necessary to be represented there. During my investigation of this matter I have come to the conclusion that if all the oil contained in the pipe line were to go direct from the Alberta oil fields to the tank farm in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, the excess to be exported would command the employment of over 500 men, day in and day out, 365 days a year. The estimated payroll would be in the vicinity of $5,000 a day, $150,000 a month, almost $2 million a year, and this all in extra wages to the people of British Columbia, with all that means to our economy; and yet the attorney general of British Columbia does not think it is important to defend his province at the hearing on this application. If this is Social Credit, thank God I am a Liberal.

105,000	people, and I have taken this opportunity to make my complaint. I think the attorney general should have been represented there at least. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the private debate is over I wish to make a few remarks. Following the example of the last speaker, I wish to refer to a matter that has been brought to my attention today, before I go on with the other matter that has been engaging the attention of the house for some time.
The matter to which 1 wish to refer has been mentioned by previous speakers. They have been receiving letters from the municipalities in their constituencies with reference to discrimination in taxation between the provinces and the municipalities. I also have received communications along these lines, and I wish to state my case as others have done before, before making my budget remarks.
The Budget-Mr. McLure
The city of Charlottetown is the capital of our province; it is also the seat of the provincial government itself. It also contains the heads of all the departments of the federal government. Conditions have arisen between the municipality, or the capital city there, and the provincial government similar to that of other provinces. I refer to the purchasing of supplies and goods that are used by the governments either of the city or of the provinces. The class of goods that are bought and on which the sales tax is rebated in so far as the province is concerned is similar to those goods which are bought by the municipal government. The city of Charlottetown municipality should have the same privileges extended to them as are extended to the provincial government with respect to the remission or rebate of sales tax on goods purchased by the provincial government.
I hope this matter will be taken up by the government, and that they will cease the injustices and discriminations with regard to the municipalities, and particularly the city of Charlottetown in whose behalf I am speaking. I am sure it would be much better for the government to give consideration to this request than to be pushed into making the proper adjustments later on.
We come now to that part of the budget which has occupied the attention of this house for quite a number of days. This debate allows great latitude and hon. members can speak on almost any subject. If time permits I intend to refer to a few things of vital importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
The budget was presented to the house on Thursday, February 19, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). If I was trying to find something to describe that occasion, I think I would take the minister's initials, "D.C.A.", and say "Douglas Can Act". The minister did an excellent piece of acting from the script which had been placed before him. The minister made one statement at the opening of his speech which I think put all hon. members at ease, and I quote from page 2115 of Hansard of February 19 as follows:
With the common consent of all groups in this house the work of this session has been planned so as to begin and conclude our deliberations six or eight weeks ahead of the usual times-
What a hope!
-so that adjournment can take place well in advance of the date appointed by Her Majesty for her coronation.
That was a most important statement because it indicated that we would not be having an April election, at least this year. I have listened to at least a score of budget addresses and I do not believe that in all
2918	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. McLure that time I have seen a larger attendance. The galleries were filled to overflowing. As one looked into the faces of those who had come to hear the minister deliver his budget speech, one could see they were radiant with hope and expectation; but at its conclusion, when you again looked into the faces of those people, you saw nothing but disappointment and despair. There was nothing for them to take home; there was no hope or relief.
One heard many remarks about the budget. One remark I overheard in the elevator was this: It is time for the opposition to take over the national financial mess in this country and see what they can do for us. There were many other remarks, but that was an outstanding one.
It is interesting to note that many of the great civilized nations of the world have made changes in their governments. Great Britain has now a Conservative government led by that greatest of world statesmen, Winston Churchill. The great republic to the south has a new government in office. No doubt those two countries are looking to see a change of government in the third great nation as soon as the next election comes around. We hope that that change will come at a time when these other two great nations have proper governments in office.
Time does not permit me to refer in detail to all the speeches that have been made during this debate, but I shall refer to a few. There have been 75 or more speeches during the present debate. Because of his years of experience the Minister of Finance was able to give an uplift, or, as some would say, a face-lifting to the budget which he presented. However, he was followed by the financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell); and after he had finished, the budget looked more like a wreck than ever because the hon. member had torpedoed it from all sides. I should like to record again the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood. It has been recorded already by several hon. members, but I think it is important enough to record again. As reported on page 2348 of Hansard of February 24, 1953, the hon. member moved:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question he deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that under the present budget the government proposes to take more money from the taxpayers of Canada than ever before for non-defence and defence expenditures without any effective steps being taken to:
(a) deal with waste, extravagance and administrative inefficiency; (b) give tax relief to those who need it most; (c) offer any encouragement to Canadian farmers in meeting the serious consequences of lost markets and lower prices resulting


from the government's agricultural and marketing policies; (d) permit an independent inquiry into the organization accounting and administration of the Department of National Defence."
Following the hon. member for Greenwood, the leader of the C.C.F. group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well), made his presentation. After denouncing the budget he said he could see nothing objectionable in the amendment moved by the financial critic. He accepted that amendment but he moved an amendment to the amendment to be found on page 2354 of Hansard. I think it is all to the good that I should include it in my remarks. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"This house further regrets that the present budget is a rich man's budget which:
(1)	makes tax cuts retroactive to January 1st for corporations but not for individual Canadians;
(2)	doubles the exemption levels for the full corporation tax rate while leaving exemption levels for individual Canadians unchanged: and
(3)	doubles the credits allowed to shareholders for dividends, but gives no comparable credits to those who do the work that produces the dividends."
There is another leader of a group who has condemned the budget in his own language and has moved an amendment to the amendment which seems to be very satisfactory when taken with the amendment. The next speaker was from the Social Credit group. He spoke at considerable length and like the other two speakers he denounced the new budget as one which benefited those who needed tax relief the least and left the major burden still on the lower and middle income people who have to pay the taxes. All these speakers denounced the tax changes as an attempt to woo the voters before a general election. The leader of the Social Credit party stated that it was a shameless repetition of the tax cuts made prior to 1949.
After that criticism, there came to the rescue of the dilapidated budget the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. This new assistant was one of the few men in Ottawa who had the privilege of assisting in preparing the budget from its very beginning, and he was in a position to be well informed about the budget. However, when his speech was finished, the appearance of the budget in the eyes of the public had not improved so far as its beauty was concerned, and it was still in the down-and-out class.
A moment ago I stated that I have listened to more than 20 different budget speeches in the house. In making that statement, I am reminded of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. MARCH 13, 1953
Gardiner) because he expressed himself similarly. He said that he had listened to many budgets, and that the present budget reminded him of another one which he named. His remarks are recorded on page 2665 of Hansard of March 5, and I wish to refer to them for a moment or two. The minister referred to a certain time in the government of this country that appealed to him as possibly giving rise to some good Grit propaganda. He told how he came into the house. He described his actions quite vividly, as can be seen from page 2665 of Hansard to which I referred. He told about crawling into the gallery and finally hiding behind a post there. I find it hard to understand how the Minister of Agriculture, as we know him today, could be so shy, so frightened, so depressed that he had to crawl into the gallery and hide when he got in there. I think he must have been either overrating or underrating himself at that time. However, he got in. I heard that same budget speech, but I must say that I did not have to crawl in and I did not have to hide when I did get in. I was elected by the good people of Queens county and I sat in seat No. 21 while the Minister of Agriculture was hiding behind a post.
However, that is not the point I want to make with regard to his speech. He went into great details about what he saw that day in the house. He described the dress of the then prime minister and the other members of the cabinet. A few moments ago a person sitting in the gallery looking down upon the cabinet members then in the house would have seen one member of the cabinet asleep, another dozing with his feet up where his elbows should be and the right hon. gentleman ready to go out. That is a contrast to what he has described as the wonderful dress of the cabinet of 1930.

Wait a moment. You can have your say when I am through. I am not in any humour to be interrupted right now. There is one point the Minister of Agriculture made with respect to Mr. Bennett's speech with which I agree. He said that it was a good speech. It was a good speech, made by the great statesman of the time, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who was also minister of finance. The Minister of Agriculture could have gone further and said that it was a most remarkable speech made at a time when the country needed a great statesman like Mr. Bennett to make such a speech to bring confidence back to at least some of the people of Canada during the 68108-186
The Budget-Mr. McLure depression that had been laid at the doorstep of the Conservative party by the Liberals when they went out of power.

speechtext: What was the reason for the Minister of Agriculture making the very nice remark that he made? It was just his subtle way of bringing before the house and possibly before the country the years from 1930 to 1935. He did bring them up in that same old ragtime Grit way, singing that old song: "From 1930 to 1935".

speechtext:
Just keep quiet there now.
Then he proceeded to blast some Grit figures regarding low prices of 1930 to 1935. Where he discovered those statistics 1 do not know, but I do not think anybody in the house believed them, and I do not think the right hon. gentleman himself believed them.
I was going to deal with these figures in detail but that is not necessary. All I want to do is place on the record what an hon. member, a neighbour of his from the west, had to say. I refer there to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), and I want the two sets of figures close enough to each other that the public can read them both at the one time. On page 2666 of Hansard the Minister of Agriculture made this statement:
The export price of wheat during that period-
That is the period he was referring to before, 1930 to 1935.
-averaged 68 cents a bushel . . . and cattle averaged $61.93 a head.
He emphasized the latter part by saying:
That was not a hundredweight or a pound, although they have been up to about half that per hundredweight recently. It was $61.93 a head.
Well, as I said a moment ago, I do not know where he discovered those figures but he used them anyhow.
The hon. minister was very anxious to have those figures strongly on the record, and he repeated them because he wanted to show what had been done under the Bennett government from 1930 to 1935. It must have been a great surprise to the Grit minister when the hon. member for Assiniboia put the skids right under his figures. The hon. member's figures will be found on page 2681 of Hansard, and I cannot read them all, since that would take too much time, but I will read a few of them. Here is what he said:
The thing that amazed me in the statistics he gave about prices was that during the Conservative

The Budget-Mr. McLure regime prices were so much better than prices during part of the time after the Liberal government took office.
A little further on he said:
At any rate, $69 was the price under the Bennett government. The present Minister of Agriculture and this government came to power in 1935.
I am still quoting from what the hon. member for Assiniboia said.
What happened to cattle prices in 1937? The members1 . . . know very well that under a Liberal government ... at Ottawa, with the present Minister of Agriculture, . . . the farmers in Saskatchewan were forced to sell many cattle for a cent a pound, $10 a head.
Further on he said:
The government here paid a cent a pound; that is what it paid. I know of one farmer who sold two head of cattle for $21-
I am quoting these figures because I want them recorded close to those given by the Minister of Agriculture.

The hon. member for

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To the support of the budget that has been so ruthlessly kicked around came the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). We thought that he would support the budget in the best manner he knew but he did not wish to speak on the budget,
[Mr. McLure.1

supporting it or otherwise, as far as I can understand. He did want to give us a report on that luxurious trade conference upon which they had been frolicking down among the Latin American countries. I must say now that, if the members of the conference party all looked as well when they returned as did the Minister of Trade and Commerce, they must have had a whale of a good time. He went on to tell what a wonderful conference it was. He did not say that the taxpayers of the country were paying for the fun they had, but he tried to leave the impression that they had done a great deal of good. He said that in this conference they had made a lot of new friends. Why wouldn't they? They were going where they were not known.
Had I known that they were going down there I could have told them where they could get some business. It is all very well to get these flowery reports about what they do when they get out making contacts, but Mr. Speaker, I would like to have placed on the record here by the Minister of Trade and Commerce one item of business which they transacted; one sale of any one commodity that Canada has to sell.
Had I known they were going I could have given them one of the best opportunities-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everybody else knew they were going.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Easy now, boy.
The best opportunity they had was to unload some 20,000 silver fox skins which the government has been trying to market for the past three or four years. We always had a fairly good trade in South America for this article. This government, and the Liberal government preceding it, ruined that market by their unjust form of taxation on furs. If this delegation had desired to do so, they could have sold these furs for their own government because they had the right to sell them at any price they wished. If they could not sell them, why did they not do as the natives did years ago and barter them for some articles for which Canada had some use?
This delegation might have stopped at Washington on the way home, where they could have taken up the matter of duty on furs going into the United States. Silver fox furs from the United States enter Canada free of duty. When we ship silver fox furs into the United States we are met at the border with a 37J per cent ad valorem duty, which is practically prohibitive. If they had even done that little bit of good while they were away gallivanting, we would have had a little blessing for them instead of perhaps cursing them. However, we are not going to deal too harshly with them.

I could not help but be amused at one remark made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he told us of a place in which the government could spend some money. As I understand it, it was to help build seaports in Mexico so that we could develop trade. If this government wants to find a place in which to invest their money instead of sinking it in something of that kind, I shall tell them where they can invest their money and it will bring wonderful returns. I refer them to the Andrew Rae Duncan commission, a commission appointed by the Liberals in 1926. One of the recommendations in that report refers to seaports and to the harbour of Charlottetown. The commission suggested that the port of Charlottetown be put in such shape that it could take care of all ships that are coming in there from time to time, and not have them anchoring outside the harbour because of unsatisfactory accommodation in the harbour, as they have to do on some occasions.
I want to mention another place in which they could invest their money by following out the instructions of their own commission. This suggestion is made on behalf of labour in the city of Charlottetown as well as on behalf of trade. Why would the government not build, as we have urged and coaxed them to do from time to time, a railway marine slip so that we could take care of our own ships? Today, we can do the top work on any ship but we have not accommodations to take care of work under the water line. For instance, we have six large ships of our own and we have quite a few smaller ones. All these vessels have to be sent to Quebec, Halifax or Saint John to have work done. One of them, valued at some $4 million or $5 million, was lost while making the trip for repairs. If we had had our own railway marine slip, as we should have, that vessel might not have been lost. If we had this slip, we could employ over 200 men the year round, instead of our labour having to leave for other places. We have machine shops; we have mechanics and we have labour, all of which can do any of the work required in repairing any ship that floats. I think that this hon. gentleman will yet have to give us some consideration. I believe he should have mentioned this himself, because it had been previously brought to his attention by the provincial government before he left on this trip.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I might say a few words with reference to our own conditions and the things that we really require in the constituency of Queens. The budget has not given us any relief whatever in that province. The riches of the province are not pyramided, as 68108-1864
The Budget-Mr. Bryce they are in some of the other provinces in which there are men of great wealth. There are none of these rich men to benefit from this budget. We pay our share of taxes, and the people in my constituency who pay the taxes receive practically no relief from this budget. I want to say that one class who came up here with a petition and who should have received consideration was the blind people. We all have sympathy for them and they should have received further consideration from the government.
I want to say a few words about another class of people we have, and that is the incapacitated.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am obliged to inform him that his time has expired.

speechtext:
May I be allowed two or three minutes to finish this one item? As I said, we have a number of incapacitated people. A resolution concerning the incapacitated was presented to this house, and I was sorry that it did not come to a final vote. This is a problem with which the government will yet have to deal, along with the problem of pensioners in the lower brackets. Before I came to Ottawa I received a telephone call from a pensioner. He was a railway man who had retired on the old pension scheme. He was a thrifty character, and he had saved a few dollars. His pension was $80 per month, which has only the purchasing power of about $37, so he had to dip into his savings to such an extent that today those savings are exhausted. He does not know what to do. He said to me, "Well, the only thing I can look forward to now is the poorhouse."
There are other matters with which I should have liked to deal, but I suppose there will be an opportunity when the estimates come before us. I thank you for the little extension of time, but I thought perhaps you would have given me half an hour longer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after having listened to over 60 members speaking in the budget debate, it is rather difficult to get to one's feet and speak on the budget without repeating what someone else has already said.
I agree with the leader of this group when
he said that this budget provides greater benefits to those in the upper income brackets than to those in the lower brackets. Many speakers on the opposition side of the house have referred to the budget as a rich man's budget. Let us consider for a few moments the average taxpayer with two children who earns $2,400 a year and who in 1952 paid $19, including social security tax. In 1953 the same

The Budget-Mr. Bryce taxpayer will pay $18 or will have a saving of a mere $1 for the year. Let us take the case of the married taxpayer with two children, earning $3,000. In 1952 he paid $130, including social security tax. In 1953 he will pay $126, $4 less than a year ago.
On the other hand we find a different story when we examine the savings of those in the upper income brackets. The taxpayer receiving an income of $20,000 will benefit in 1953 to the extent of $360. But of all the concessions made by the minister, perhaps the most astonishing one is the example that a married man with no dependents, who receives all his income from dividends from Canadian corporations and companies, is exempt from paying a personal income tax until he is receiving $9,760. If this $9,760 were earned by a married farmer, businessman or merchant, with no children, he would be liable to an income thx payment of $1,657.60. But because the other fellow is a shareholder in Canadian companies and receives all his income from that source, he does not have to pay a single cent of personal income tax. If he has a further $10,000 of unearned income, he would have a further 20 per cent credit or a $2,000 deduction from any tax on that additional $10,000.
The argument of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), of course, is that this money has already been taxed. It has been taxed on a corporation basis but not on an individual basis; and of course it would lead to double taxation. Let us take, for example, a married man with no dependents, who has investment income from dividend paying stocks of $9,760. He has, of course, the usual personal exemption of $2,000. After deducting the $2,000, that would mean a taxable income of $7,760, if it were earned. He would pay income tax on an earned income in this way: On the first $6,000 he would pay $1,140; on the remaining $1,760, where the tax is on a basis of 26 per cent, he would pay $457.60, making a total of $1,597.60. Then he would have to pay the social security tax of $60, or a total of $1,657.60 if it were earned.
This man, of course, would have a surtax on investment income over $2,400. He has an exemption of $2,400. If we deduct that from $9,760, he has to pay surtax on $7,360 at the rate of 4 per cent, which would mean that he would pay $294.40. Therefore the total tax would be $1,952 if he were paying it on the basis of earned income. But since he gets this money unearned, from other sources, from stock dividends, he is entitled to deduct 20 per cent of $9,760 or $1,952 from the tax he would otherwise have to pay; and that is the exact amount that he would have paid as personal income tax if he had earned it.


I know that it is quite easy to be critical when speaking on a budget. But when the minister could afford to do without the extra taxation which I think he said amounted to about $250 million, it would have been nice for him to have done something for the people who are receiving pensions for the blind. The removal of the means test with respect to blind persons would have been a boon to those people who are obliged to live in darkness through no fault of their own. It is to be hoped that in the near future some government will remove the means test from the pension for the blind.
Then there is the means test in connection with the war veterans allowance recipients. These are the men who are old before their time. These are the men who marched away in world war I. We can remember what we said at that time, namely that nothing would be good enough for them when they came back. We now find among them some cases of great hardship which the Minister of Finance could have helped at this time with the assistance of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe).
Then there is that class of people who, through no fault of their own, are unable to earn their own livelihood; they are dependent upon their parents to keep and to clothe them. We have the case of the paralytic, the person who is permanently crippled. There are those who are crippled from arthritis and there are many cases of chronic illness.
On various occasions we have had representations from people in wheel chairs who spoke on behalf of persons such as these. Of course, in giving these people relief, the provincial government would have to be considered. But it certainly would have been nice if the dominion government had done something to lead the way.
At this time I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to the Manitoba Association for Retarded Children, in order to see whether he could provide a grant as an aid to education or whether the money could be granted in any other way. I bring this matter to the minister's attention inasmuch as it is one of the things that would have to be done on a federal-provincial basis. I have the brief here but it is too long to read at this time. There are more than 800 of these children in Manitoba; they are children with an I.Q. between 40 and 60, now living at home with their parents, and not urgently requiring to be in an institution. They are really a forgotten group. The department of education makes it an offence punishable by a fine for the

parents to send them to the regular classes in school. Children who are blind and children who are deaf are educated or trained at provincial expense. Children whose affliction is mental have equal right to education and some kind of training that will help them to fit into the community. May I, Mr. Speaker, just quote a couple of paragraphs from their brief? This is the brief they presented to the department of education in Manitoba:
That we petition the department of education and the department of health to provide day school and special training classes for mentally retarded children who are living at home by:
Extending the Public School Act to provide that in any school district where there are at least fifteen children of school age who are mentally retarded, but who are deemed by the provincial psychiatrist to be capable of benefiting from special instruction, it shall be compulsory for that district to provide the special instruction required.
Exploring terms of the health education and mental health grants now provided by the department of national health at Ottawa through the provincial department of health to see if some of these moneys can be spent to provide the supplementary grants required for such classes and to provide intelligence testing services so that there is proper screening of children for these classes and to pay scholarships to Manitoba teachers to take special training for this work.
I might say that I have a niece in Scotland who has been specially trained in the work of taking up these classes, and they have done a wonderful job for some children who have a low I.Q. I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance will give it the consideration that it deserves.
Today I received a letter from the tariff board with the result of appeal No. 284. This was an appeal by the Dow Chemical Company against the Department of National Revenue. Evidently, from the evidence I have read, different chemicals are used to make antifreeze, and they were being admitted duty-free under tariff item 208h. The Dow Chemical Company appealed, asking that a 20 per cent duty be applied to these imports used in the manufacture of antifreeze. I have always understood that it was the policy of the Liberal government to decrease tariffs, not increase them. This is something to which the government should give further study, because Canadians are paying about $2 a gallon more for antifreeze than are our neighbours to the south. Residents of the west in general, and in my own constituency in particular, are going to be most annoyed about this decision. Antifreeze of different blends is used in all cars, trucks and tractors in the west, and the western farmer and other users have always complained about the high price compared with the United States price.

In an extensive study prepared for the New York stock exchange by the Brookings Institution of Washington it was determined that on March 1, 1952 there were 6,490,000 individuals holding shares in publicly-owned corporations. When talking about unearned income the argument is always put up about the widow who has her money invested and would be deprived of her livelihood. I come now to the implement companies. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has defended them and has told the house that they needed this advance. Personally I cannot see that they do. I notice from the papers of April, 1938, that the shares of Cockshutt Plow were quoted at 7 while the shares of Massey-Harris were quoted at 5], I shall not give the quotations for the shares of other companies, as I think these two are sufficient for my purpose. By April 2 of this year the shares of Cockshutt Plow had advanced to 163 while those of Massey-Harris had come up to 17[. According to today's paper there was a further increase, Cockshutt shares being quoted at 173 and Massey-Harris at 181.
I admit that I know more about livestock than this sort of stock, but it seems to me that these companies must be in a sound financial position when there is this improvement in the value of their shares on the stock market. These increases show that there must be an expectancy of greater profits in the future.
I think what I said then has been amply proved by the continued rise in the earnings of these companies, which have gone on making more and more money. I should like to refer to an advertisement by Massey-Harris in Maclean's of March 1, 1953 in which they set out some dominion bureau of statistics figures. These deal with a number of items such as raw materials, average hourly rates, farm products, farm wage rates, but I should like to refer particularly to what is said about farm implements, and I quote:
Yet in this same period the index for Massey-Harris Canadian-made farm implements has risen only 66-5 per cent.
That may be quite true, but they are including farm implements the price of which has not risen very much. They went up some, but they have not gone up as much. Take the plow, the cultivator and the double disc, implements that we do not use nearly as much today as we did ten years ago. Their prices have not increased as much as the prices of combines, tractors and one-way discs. Therefore this advertisement, while it may be right in the mind of the man who wrote it, to my

way of thinking is not a fair comparison. I have said already that some tractors are more than double what they were. Combines are away up in price. A combine in 1944, such as we owned on our farm, cost $2,800. Today a similar combine is over $6,000. One-way discs are also away up in price.
One thing the advertisement does not say is how much the profits of the company have gone up since 1941. I have not the profits for 1941 but I have the profits, after taxes, in 1943. They were $1,322,357. In 1952 they made $10,868,600, and the year before they made more than that. I know that the company has to have a profit and that it is worldwide in its scope. I have seen Massey-Harris machinery in operation not only in Canada but in the British Isles, on the continent of Europe and in New Zealand and Australia. They are a tremendously big organization. But when I look at these returns I am convinced that the large implement companies are taking more than the traffic will bear or, in other words, they are charging too much for the implements.

In 1936-37 a committee was set up to inquire into the cause of high prices of farm implements, and I wish to quote the following from page 1264 of the proceedings of the special committee on farm implements:
The committee Is of the opinion, as a result of the above finding, that there is competition in the matter of securing sales but little or no effective competition in the matter of prices as between companies. It is true that one company cannot increase its price unless other companies, particularly the larger ones, follow suit but, as illustrated in January, 1936, and throughout the period, increases in the prices, or maintenance of prices when a decrease should have been expected, occurs simultaneously in all the companies. The companies insist that no understanding existed between them in the matter of the January, 1936 increase and that the increases resulted from the same conditions arising in each company. It is extremely difficult for the committee to understand the remarkable coincidence of the increase occurring in the same month of the same year and, generally speaking on the same implements and to the same extent.
The companies state that it is the practice in the industry to exchange price lists and it may well be that this practice enables the companies to quickly gain uniformity in the matter of price levels. The lack of free price competition in this industry, as in many other industries, is one of the real problems of modern economic life. From the standpoint of the business executives, free price competition was not a satisfactory condition and escape from it was one of the salient reasons for the formation of large corporate units by amalgamation of smaller previously existing companies. From the consumer's standpoint, however, it is apparent that this has resulted in higher and less flexible prices for the commodities which he has to purchase.
Then in 1952 a special select committee on farm implements sat in Saskatchewan. The
The Budget-Mr. Bryce work of this committee was not too successful. In their efforts to obtain a true picture of the operations of the farm implement industry they failed to get the co-operation of the large companies to supply the information they needed. May I quote from the final report of the 1952 special select committee on farm implements of the province of Saskatchewan. It reads in part as follows:
Your committee regrets to report that it has been unable to complete its task as fully and adequately as it had hoped, due to its failure to obtain specific information deemed fundamental to the inquiry. Despite repeated assurances of their desire to co-operate, the four manufacturing companies have been most dilatory in returning answers to questions relating to factory costs submitted to them on January 26, 1952. These questions remain unanswered to date, and repeated requests have been met by pleas for more time: in one case by a direct refusal to comply.
The committee cannot but record its sense of frustration and impotence in confrontation with this attitude of these extra-provincial companies. It feels that a principle is involved-a principle which merits consideration and study by all provincial legislatures and by the parliament of Canada.
The situation apparently is that companies, with head offices located in another province, yet doing a great volume of their Canadian business in this province, can take advantage of the immunity their location confers to deny a committee of this legislature information material to an inquiry undertaken in the public interest, and essential to an adequate report on the matters under study and review. These companies too are shielded by another immunity. As Canadian incorporations engaged in interprovincial trade, they are immune from retaliatory action by the province which might be construed as in restraint of that trade.
I think the government should set up a special committee to investigate the farm implement industry so that information which certain implement companies refused to give to the committee that sat in Saskatchewan in 1952 could be obtained. Then we would know if the farmer is being charged a fair price for his implements or if the companies are charging too much.
If we could have such a committee or inquiry, the committee could also go into the standardization of farm implements. When it is a good thing to standardize our arms in wartime, surely it is high time to talk about the standardization of our farm implements. Not only would the parts be exchangeable but the companies could build better implements and cut down selling costs. If farm prices are to come down, something will have to be done about it, and one of the first things to do would be to set up a committee of the house to go into these matters affecting farm implements. I appeal to the government to set up a special committee to go into farm implement prices. Indications point to lower farm produce prices, and farmers will not be able to buy farm machinery at present prices.
