Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the occasion of taking part in this debate. I wanted to speak earlier, but owing to the geographical position of Russell county, which I have the honour of representing, I have the pleasure of receiving large numbers of its nice citizens at my office in the house. That is why I have been unable to express my opinions sooner in the nouse. I always take pleasure in receiving my electors and strive to obtain what they want, wherever they may come from, whatever may be their racial origin, their religion or their political allegiance.
The county I have the honour of representing is typical of Canada as a whole, because its population is made up of people of various races, various creeds and various classes of society. A little more than half of them are city people; this includes several thousand most distinguished and competent civil servants, who serve the country well, for it has been proven that Canadian civil servants are the most efficient a country could have. Several hundred others are employed by the public works department, the queen's printer, the national research council, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, etc. I know they rank among the best employees this country can wish for. There are a great many businessmen and industrialists, as well as some of the most highly-skilled workers to be found anywhere. Let us not forget the thousands of farmers who own beautiful up-to-date farms; most of them have electricity, automobiles, tractors and enjoy all the conveniences that electricity can bring into our modern homes. We. the Liberals, are administering this country in order to enable the people to live well and get those modern conveniences, if they do not have them already.
During the last ten years, the population of Russell has more than doubled, increasing at the rate of more than 3,000 citizens a year. I am pleased with it and I will give but one example, that of Manor Park, a smart suburb of more than 5,000, with modern homes and a very distinguished population. Six years ago, a few houses only could be found at that place. Eastview, barely ten years ago, had a population of 5,000. It now goes oeyond the 16,000 mark. There can be found most modern houses, spacious stores and theatres and hotels which are the envy of the large cities of this country, and even of other distant countries where I had the pleasure of travelling with my family last summer.
Then there is the headquarters of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a police force recognized to be without t>eer in the world


for competence and effectiveness. It occupies finer quarters than any other police force, anywhere. I would invite my colleagues to pay them a visit. They may be found in Overbrook, a short distance from here.
The Department of Transport, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the national research council and the Department of National Defence, either at Uplands or on the Montreal road, at Rockcliffe, at Greely, have brought various improvements to the two airpoi'ts; they have erected different buildings, married quarters for the armed forces, especially for the R.C.A.F., and modern schools. I would like the members of this house to visit these improvements. They are a source of pride to all Canadians. They allow our civil servants or military personnel to give better service. Moreover, the erection of these various buildings has given jobs to thousands of workers. Approximately $8 million yearly have been spent there since the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, in 1950.
Everyone here is familiar with the Rockcliffe airport, one of the most up-to-date in Canada from the point of view of defence, as well as with the Uplands airport which will be shortly one of the most modern from the point of view both of defence and transport.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) for the ability he has shown in the improvement of these airports as well as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) for the active part he has taken in the improvement of Uplands airport and elsewhere.
I should like, however, to draw the attention of the Minister of National Defence, whom I was congratulating a moment ago for his participation in the construction of buildings and schools of the most modern type-as I did orally and by correspondence- on the necessity of arriving at some kind of agreement with the Ontario government, whereby the latter could amend the law if necessary, so that the children of our fliers may have the educational opportunities to which they are entitled. In order to do so, both a public school and a separate school are necessary. If the parents who wish to send their children to public schools are entirely free to do so, it ought to be the same for the parents who want to send theirs to separate schools. There is no reason for the present situation, which does not give justice to anyone. In my opinion, it would be easy to solve the problem; let us divide the present school in two; part of it would be the public school and the other part, the

separate school. If there be a lack of space, more must be added. But would it not be better to build new accommodation? In my county all villages and towns have beautiful churches, and most modern schools. East-view will have a hospital which will be the pride of the capital and of the whole of Canada. This 400 bed hospital will have a most competent staff. I invite in advance my colleagues from Hull, Ottawa, Prescott, Carle-ton and Russell counties to patronize this hospital. The project will cost more than three million. The Daughters of Wisdom have accepted the task of directing the hospital, because they are eager to do even more for the sick, not being satisfied with the immense work they have accomplished in that respect in Canada and elsewhere. I want to say in this house how deep is our esteem for them and how much we are grateful for what they do. I ask divine Providence to protect their order which accomplishes so much good on this earth through their excellent work, their teaching of the young, and their endeavours to come to the aid of the unfortunate; their work is great and deserving from a religious point of view, but so often unknown to the population. The love which those sisters bestow upon the unfortunate is often unrecognized and their good deeds are very seldom rewarded on this earth.
People will say that such a hospital is in receipt of provincial and federal grants. It is true and it is an excellent thing. However, building costs being what they are, I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to find the means of doubling the grants paid to hospitals. I would also ask the provinces to do the same.
Now, let us come back to our schools-

Mr. Speaker, in the course of this debate there have been several suggestions from opposition members that the
13. 1953	2927
Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited government define its policy relative to the export of petroleum and natural gas. It is my purpose at this time to attempt to do so.
I think to do so will be helpful not only to members of the house but to all those interested in the production and transportation of these products.
Pernaps I had better first outline the relative responsibilities of the province of Alberta and of the federal government. Both petroleum and natural gas are, of course, the prop-produced. In the case of Alberta, that erty of the province in which they are province controls the production of gas and oil, as well as its transportation within the province and, under special legislation, controls the export of natural gas across its provincial borders. In the case of petroleum, the province	can decide whether the
petroleum shall be moved westward or eastward. In the case of natural gas, the province may determine the amount of gas to be exported, when it will be exported, and the point of exit either eastward or westward.
So far as the federal government is concerned, once the petroleum moves outside the province in which it is produced it then becomes the responsibility of the federal government to determine the destination, if it is oil moved in a pipe line, or the destination of the natural gas wherever it may go. Under the Pipe Lines Act, the board of transport commissioners has the responsibility for determining the route of pipe lines and such other responsibilities as are recited in that act. Those are responsibilities of the federal government administered by the board of transport commissioners.
Then we have another act which covers the export of petroleum and natural gas, provided it is exported by pipe line. This act is the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, which was enacted in 1907. Perhaps it would be worth while at this stage to read a few pertinent sections of that act, because its contents are sometimes misquoted. Section 1 of the act simply recites the short title, the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. Section 2 of the act is the interpretation section and reads as follows:
In this act. unless the context otherwise requires.
(a)	"export" and "exportation" mean.
(i)	when used with reference to electrical power or energy, respectively export and exportation from Canada by lines of wire or other conductor,
(ii)	when used with reference to petroleum, natural gas, water or other fluid, whether liquid or gaseous, capable of being exported, respectively export and exportation from Canada through pipe lines or other like contrivances:
(b)	"fluid" means petroleum, natural gas. water or other fluid, whether liquid or gaseous, capable of being exported by means of pipe lines or other like contrivances, and produced in Canada:
(c)	"power" means electrical power or energy produced in Canada.

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited
Then section 3 reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations not inconsistent with this act for giving effect to the object and intention thereof, and by such regulations may impose fees to be paid thereunder by applicants for licences or others.
Such regulations shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after the making thereof, or, if parliament is not then in session, within fifteen days after the opening of the next session thereof.
Section 4 mentions the payment of duties and the duration of the licence. Section 5 reads:
No person shall export any power or fluid without a licence, or any power or fluid in excess of the quantity permitted by his licence, or otherwise -than as permitted by such licence.
2. No person shall, without a licence, construct or place in position any line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
The next section deals with the licence to export. Section 6 reads:
Subject to any regulations of the governor in *council in that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences, upon such conditions as he thinks proper, for the exportation of power or fluid where a right to export exists by lawful authority.
2. Such licence shall be revocable upon such notice to the licensee as the governor in council deems reasonable in each case.
Section 7 reads:
Any such licence may provide that the quantity of power or fluid to be exported shall be limited to the surplus, after the licensee has supplied for distribution to customers for use in Canada power or fluid to the extent defined by such licence, at prices and in accordance with conditions, rules and regulations prescribed by the governor in council.
2. Every such licence shall be revocable at will by the governor in council if the licensee refuses or neglects to comply with any of the conditions imposed with regard to the supply and distribution of power or fluid in Canada.
The remaining sections of the act relate to penalties for violations of the act.
A distinction must be made between exports of petroleum and exports of natural gas. Petroleum is a commodity which moves freely across all international boundaries, as does iron ore, wheat and certain other basic commodities. The refiner buys his petroleum wherever he can buy it cheapest. He may buy today from Alberta, tomorrow from Venezuela, the next day from the Middle East and the next day from the United States, depending upon where he can make the best arrangement. No problem of continuous supply is involved. If one source becomes no longer available, the refiner may buy from another source. Petroleum can be moved in tanker ships, tank cars or tank wagons, and in such event its export from Canada is not under government control. In other words, as I have pointed out, petroleum moving


in the manner I have just stated does not come under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
Movement by pipe line is under government export control, but this does not alter the fact that there is no obligation imposed upon the government of Canada to maintain a continuous supply. Canada's national policy should therefore be, first, to move petroleum from the source of production to refineries within economic distance in the cheapest possible way; second, to arrange for markets for that portion of the Canadian output that cannot be economically used in Canadian refineries in the market that offers the highest return to the producer. This is the policy this government has followed and intends to follow.
Pursuant to that policy, the Interprovincial pipe line has been built from Edmonton to Superior, Wisconsin, serving refineries at Moose Jaw, Regina and Winnipeg. The present route involves movement of the petroleum from Superior, Wisconsin, to Sarnia, Ontario, by lake tankers. The entire movement from Edmonton to Sarnia is in bond, except for permits that have been granted to export small quantities of petroleum to the United States.
Interprovincial Pipe Line is presently engaged in extending this pipe line through the United States to Sarnia with the purpose of arranging for a continuous supply at Sarnia and further lowering the cost of transportation. The "in-bond" privilege presently granted to Interprovincial will apply to the new pipe line. This is consistent with government policy of approving the lowest possible cost of transportation from the source of supply to refining centres within economic distance of the source.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and his supporters have been arguing that the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company should have been compelled to take the pipe line to Port Arthur instead of to Superior, and then build the pipe line extension to Sarnia around the north and east sides of the great lakes. It is worth noting that the distance from Gretna, Manitoba, to Sarnia by the present route is 939 miles, while the distance by the route advocated by the Leader of the Opposition is 1,341 miles. The cost increase involved in building the pipe line following the latter route would result in an additional expenditure estimated at $67 million. Such a line would touch no important refining centre and thus would be of no important value to the area it would traverse. Remembering that the cost of the line must eventually be paid either by the producers or by the users of gasoline and other petroleum

products, or by both, the government is not disposed to exercise its authority to saddle these consumers with an additional and unnecessary $67 million of expenditure, nor would the national interest be served by so doing.
Another petroleum pipe line is being built from Edmonton to Vancouver to serve oil refineries in that important distributing centre. Application has been made by the pipe-line company for a branch line to the northwestern Pacific states. Here again such a branch line does not violate government policy, provided the refineries at Vancouver will first obtain an adequate supply of petroleum from Alberta.
We now come to a discussion of government policy related to the distribution and sale of natural gas. Here we are dealing with energy similar in many ways to electrical energy, in that export under conditions that call for investment in another country obligates Canada to maintain a continuous supply of that energy. Therefore the policy that has governed the export of electrical energy since 1907 must apply, within reason, to the export of natural gas. Canada has consistently refused to authorize firm contracts for the export of electrical energy, and this in spite of great pressure at times from producers of electrical energy. That consistent policy has paid large dividends to the Canadian economy, in that our sources of electrical energy have been preserved to our own economy.
Therefore the policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipe line across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
As I have said, the proposal is to follow this policy, within reason. To date one exception has been made. It was made in response to a request from the director of defence mobilization of the United States that Canada supply a defence production requirement for gas in order to maintain the production of copper at Anaconda's smelter in Montana. The requirement was small and of a temporary character. The government of Alberta agreed with the federal government that this defence requirement warranted a temporary deviation from the policy that both governments favour, and consequently a permit was issued, both by Alberta and by the federal government, for the export of not more than 40 million cubic feet per day or 10 billion cubic feet in any year for this purpose during a period of five years from April 7, 1951. At the end
13, 1953	2929

This government has now been confronted by a second situation which requires special attention at this time, as hearings are now in progress before the federal power commission of the United States. There has for some years been an urgent requirement for natural gas for the industrial area of British Columbia. Large reserves of natural gas have been established in northern British Columbia and in adjacent territory in northern Alberta. The natural outlet for this gas is the Pacific coast. Without that outlet it is difficult to find any economical use for gas from this northern area. The province of Alberta therefore has issued an export licence to Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, who propose to build a pipe line from that territory to Vancouver and to other consuming centres in British Columbia. Unfortunately the present and foreseeable demand within British Columbia is not in itself sufficient to justify the building of the required pipe line.
There is, however, a shortage of energy in the northwestern states adjacent to British Columbia. For a long time the United States members of the joint industrial mobilization committee of the United States and Canada have been pressing the Canadian members of the committee to arrange for delivery of natural gas from Canada into that area. The provinces of Alberta and British Columbia are convinced that supplies from the areas designated to serve the Pacific coast are ample to guarantee a substantial export of gas to the northwestern states and, in addition,, to serve the present and future needs of British Columbia. This opinion has been confirmed by petroleum experts of the federal government.
Therefore the government has issued an export permit to Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, in terms appropriate with the supply situation in the designated area. While this permit is renewable from year to year, the Canadian government accepts the responsibility of providing gas in quantities specified in the licence granted under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act for the full period of the export licence issued by the province of Alberta, assuming that Westcoast Transmission will live up to its obligation to supply customers in British Columbia.

The federal government has accepted this responsibility only after specific assurance from its own experts that it is in position physically to do so, and in recognition of the fact that this is the only practical way of assuring early delivery of natural gas to the industrial areas of British Columbia.
The province of Alberta is now giving consideration to making gas available for export, to move eastward from that province. In order to make the position of the federal government clear I wrote Premier Manning under date of January 2, 1953, as follows:
Dear Mr. Manning:
As I am leaving Canada for some five weeks, on a trade mission to South America, I think I should write you about the views of this department regarding the export of natural gas. You are doubtless aware that this department administers the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
We had a conversation about this subject at Sarnia, when Premier Frost was present. At that time, I stated that gas from Alberta must be available to potential customers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and in the intervening provinces, before further export of gas could be authorized. This attitude is consistent with the position that the government has taken with regard to the export of hydroelectric power for many years. You will appreciate that the supply of gas through a pipe line is analogous with the supply of electric power, in that both demand continuity of supply.
I am aware that, for the period when natural gas is first made available in Ontario and Quebec, and until the load can be built up, such a pipeline project is unlikely to be profitable, either for the producers of gas or for the owners of the pipe line. Nevertheless, there is evidence that a pipeline project for Ontario and Quebec can be worked out and that the project will be profitable over a period of years.
I am well aware that the government of Canada has no immediate concern with this problem, but I hope that it will be helpful for you to have its views before any definite decisions are taken in Alberta. We have worked in harmony to solve marketing problems associated with oil and gas up to the present, and I sincerely hope that we can continue to do so. We are both much concerned with sound development for Alberta and for Canada.
Yours sincerely,
C. D. Howe.
This letter is of course consistent with the government policy I have outlined. While the government of Alberta has proposals before it which involve the movement of gas eastward and across the United States border to Minneapolis, or through the United States to southern Ontario, permits to that end will not be granted under the terms of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. This government has reason to believe that it is economically feasible to build a gas pipe line from southern Alberta to Toronto- and Montreal, serving the intervening Canadian cities, and government policy will require that Canadian gas be used in Canada accordingly.
In licensing the export of gas from Alberta,


I am sure the government of that province will be disposed to conform with the policy of the federal government in that regard.
Attempts have been made to obtain a supply of natural gas for southern Ontario from the United States. Some years ago a pipe line from Texas was extended to the city of Windsor, Ontario, and an export permit was issued by the federal power commission of the United States. However, the permit from the commission contained this clause:
The delivery of natural gas to the Union Gas Company of Canada shall be curtailed or interrupted whenever it is required for the protection of deliveries of gas to any or all of the pipe lines customers in the United States-it being the Intention that at all times, persons and municipalities in the United States are to receive preferential service over that given to the Union Gas Company of Canada.
As a result of this clause, very little gas has been delivered to the Union Gas Company of Canada, and deliveries have been made only in the summer months. Obviously if deliveries of gas to Canada from the United States must be subject to this clause in every case, there can be no possibility of obtaining a reliable source of supply for Canada in the United States.
Suggestions have been made that an exchange of gas can be arranged; that is, gas delivered into the Pacific northwestern states can be exchanged for an equivalent supply delivered into southern Ontario from Texas. I am convinced that the rulings of the federal power commission which recognize the great and growing demand for natural gas in the United States debar any possibility of such an exchange. I am convinced, after thorough study of the matter, that the only reliable supply of natural gas for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec must be from western Canada by means of an all-Canadian pipe line.
Whether supplies of gas in southern and central Alberta are sufficient to justify a pipe line to eastern Ontario at this time is for the province of Alberta to determine. Reports that reach me lead me to believe that present proven supplies are sufficient not only to take care of the foreseeable needs of Alberta, but to supply the capacity of an economical pipeline. In any event, it seems likely that Alberta supplies later can be supplemented by supplies from Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Therefore I am hopeful that the pipeline project to eastern Canada can be undertaken in the near future.
I have outlined the situation as I see it. Hon. members opposite have been demanding a statement of government policy with regard to petroleum and natural gas, and I have-attempted to outline that policy, in the hope:

that there will, in future, be less confusion about permissible export of natural gas from Canada. I believe that the policies I have outlined will commend themselves to hon. members as consistent with government policy as established in 1907 and followed thereafter under the terms of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
Opposition members have been demanding that this government adopt their policy of Canada first. I think this government have a better policy than that, which is a policy of Canada always. Anything this government has done or may do in the field of petroleum or natural gas, or in any other government activity, is dictated by what this government believes to be in the long-range interest of the people of Canada. In carrying out that policy we keep in mind our association with the United Kingdom and with our fellow members of the British commonwealth of nations, ties of tradition and ties of trade extending over a great many years. We also keep in mind the good relations of this country with our largest customer and immediate neighbour, the United States; but no decision is made that this government does not believe to be in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole.
To me the policy "Canada first" involves the question, who comes second and who comes third? I just want to make the distinction that the policy of this government is "Canada always".

He has shown an interest in farmers generally, and particularly those of his own riding. He has advocated that the veterans of this country receive every consideration from this government.
I had a person write to me not long ago to suggest that the hon. member for Fraser Valley should be recognized by the erection of a gas pump in Chilliwack, greased with margarine and capped with a steel helmet. I am not going to speak at length, as I find that owing to the minister's statement I have had to abandon some of my notes. I repeat with emphasis that we in the C.C.F. believe that the transportation of gas and oil should be under public ownership because it presents an unusual opportunity for that type of ownership and administration. Members of this house other than those belonging to this group have given some support to that form of ownership for pipe lines. By having public ownership of oil and gas pipe lines we would be in position to ensure that the full requirements of Canadian industry and Canadian consumers would be met at all times. From the history of companies in the United States I am quite certain we would be assured of substantial surpluses. This government would have greater bargaining powers than would individual companies when it came to the question of exporting oil or gas to the United States.
The profitable aspect of this form of transportation has been amply demonstrated by the surpluses that have been shown in recent

years by companies in the United States and by the great increase in the prices of shares of companies which have simply obtained a charter and have not yet undertaken the transportation of gas or oil. Not only does the C.C.F. take this point of view. We have the support in this respect of the independent coalition member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). We often discuss these matters, and the hon. member has pointed out to us that in his opinion not only would public ownership be of great assistance to the Canadian National Railways and reduce some of the deficits, but would also give the Canadian government much greater bargaining power, when exporting oil or gas.

There is a very important principle involved. Last night I was protesting against what appeared to me to be a tremendous lack of vision on the part of the directors of our Canadian National Railways. That railway system is in the business of providing transportation and moving freight, whether it be in the form of coal, oil, gas or any other form.
The Canadian National directors are allowing this pipe line method of transportation to be laid all along their right of way. It will be in the hands of private corporations and this tremendous freight which is originating in this north country is going to provide corresponding profits. I sincerely hope that the volume of traffic will be such that the profits will be large.
That is the usual hope of the hon. member.
I think the Canadian National directors-I would not say the Minister of Transport-have been remiss in their duties and have shown an appalling lack of vision in not having investigated this proposal very carefully. I for one, and I am sure this would apply to other hon. members, would have been glad to approve the capital required to put in these pipe lines which would have provided a tremendous amount of freight revenue. I am tired of voting money to defray deficits. I should like to see the Canadian National look into this matter carefully before they permit private companies to lay transportation lines for gas and oil on their right of way. They and the Minister of Transport should look into the possibilities of this form of transportation being provided by the Canadian National system.
We heartily agree with the remarks the hon. member made at that time. I simply want to mention again our great pleasure at hearing the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) this afternoon. As a member of this group I urge the government to give consideration to the possibility of the public ownership of pipe lines that are used for the transportation of gas and oil in Canada, and by so doing assist the revenue and possibly the opportunity to make surpluses for the Canadian National system which is owned by the people of Canada.

When the debate was adjourned at five o'clock, I was saying: Let us speak of our schools. Some may say: why, our schools receive grants from the provinces. It is true. But were it not for our present prosperity, provincial revenues would be much lower.
At the time of the Conservative administration at Ottawa, provincial revenues were about one-quarter of what they are today, and most municipalities were bankrupt or nearly so; thousands of workers were unemployed and among those that had employment many were getting only 5, 10 or 15 cents per hour. It was at that time that so many of our farmers and businessmen went bankrupt and that quite a few industries had to shut down.
Today, over five million people have permanent employment-and if we include our professionals, our industrialists, our businessmen and our farmers, we have a total of some six million people of all classes drawing a larger income than ever before in Canada or in any other country of the world, except perhaps the country of our American friends.
I challenge our opponents to say that they ever dreamed that Canada would attain such a degree of development and prosperity. Yet, my good friends of the opposition keep on repeating that this country is not prosperous. Be serious! Don't take our Canadian citizens for people who cannot differentiate between truth and falsehood. You had the proof in 1949 and you will get still further and better proof at the next general election.
The citizens of Canada are intelligent enough and sufficiently educated to tell the difference between truth and falsehood. I repeat, our Canadian citizens are intelligent and well educated. They receive newspapers, almost all have radios and a good many of them now own television sets. Don't try to have them believe that a rabbit is as big as an elephant.
I recognize that the opposition has a very unpleasant task, but it is also a very easy task for those who don't take it seriously, because it is easy to criticize and to make requests, but it is not so easy to administer and to give. You have to be serious and your business is to provide constructive criticism. I am sorry to say that that is not the case. Most Canadians share my opinion on that point.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on his seventh budget, in which 

he announces another surplus, although this surplus is not as considerable as before, since half the budget is for national defence and millions more go for social services, that is for pensions for our veterans, our older people, our blind citizens, for family allowances, for hospital and university grants. In spite of all this, in spite of all these expenditures, the minister has managed to bring down taxes. He deserves the congratulations of all Canadians. I know that he is not particularly worried about the criticism coming from the members opposite. They criticize in spite of themselves. They know as well as we do that Canada is well administered, which is not to their liking and which explains why their criticism is so often illogical. What can you expect? They are in opposition and are sure of remaining there forever.
I also congratulate the whole cabinet which is composed of most competent men. You may be assured that my electors and myself are happy and proud to have a cabinet composed of men of such calibre.
And as for our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) what a great favour on the part of Providence to have given us a man of such destiny, whose ability can be compared with that of the greatest statesmen of any nation in any period. What a comparison between our Right Hon. Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition; one is qualified to lead and govern our country through the greatest period of prosperity of our history, and the other to remain Leader of the Opposition, until the supporters of his party succeed in replacing him, for I know there are many among them who would like to have another leader, and in fact, I wonder whether they are not going to have another one even before the elections and, if not, certainly not very long afterwards, for it is sure that the same thing will happen to him in Carleton that happened to him in the constituency he represented in 1948.
What is preventing some of them from choosing another leader immediately is the fact that they have changed so often in the past few years that they realize that instead of improving the chances of their party they have lessened them-and I share that opinion.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, some hon. members criticize the government and say that the present budget is an election budget because taxes have been reduced and radio licences abolished, etc.; some say that the government should have done more and the majority ask for grants and subsidies, pension increases, children's allowances, well,

pensions lor everybody, etc., etc. All this would cost several billions. Furthermore, they call for tax reductions which would result in a loss of revenue and an increase in expenditures of some billions of dollars. What logic!
We are blamed for having shown surpluses which have enabled us to reduce the public debt by more than $2 billion and, consequently, to cut taxes by $63 million, which is the amount of interest we would have had to pay if the public debt had not been reduced.
There are no members more anxious than we Liberals to lower taxes and to increase grants, pensions, etc. We pay taxes and we like to get subsidies and pensions just as much as our friends in the opposition; we know as well as they do that as far as the people are concerned they find it much more popular and agreeable not to pay taxes and receive benefits of all kinds.
But Canadians know that it is easier to criticize and promise than to give and administer. As a result of our perfect administration the government can pay Canadians over one billion dollars per year by way of social security measures of all kinds which did not exist some years ago in Canada while spending over two billion dollars for national defence.
I ask my hon. friends of the opposition to tell me frankly, putting aside all political considerations, whether they are not happy and satisfied with the active and important part we are playing, together with our allies who want to ensure the freedom of the citizens of their countries in the fight against the evil influence of certain nations that want, on the contrary, to destroy freedom. Who among you would rather not pay any taxes and live in slavery behind the iron curtain? If there is anyone among you or if you can find any Canadian who would rather live there, let me know and I will gladly pay his fare to Moscow, on the condition, it goes without saying, that he never be permitted to return to Canada or to any other of the free countries of the world where he could live and make use of his ability and intelligence and express his opinions in an intelligent way while respecting those of others.
No, Mr. Speaker, were it not for the $2 billion which we are forced to spend on defence because of the communist countries, we could have reduced taxes of all kinds by 50 per cent, were it not for the billion dollars spent on social services, unknown in this country twenty years ago, we could have granted a further reduction of 25 per cent; then, only 25 per cent of the present taxes
The Budget-Mr. J. O. Gour would have been left, but we would not be protected against aggression and we would be deprived of social security legislation. And yet, how wonderful it is to be able to help those of our fellow citizens who are less fortunate.
Well, our friends of the opposition should not worry, if divine Providence would allow the hostilities in Korea to come to an end, which would increase our hopes for peace, the estimates of national defence could immediately be cut by one billion. Then, we could reduce taxes by 25 per cent and increase family allowances, old age pension, and probably, unemployment insurance benefits, health insurance, and subsidies for universities and hospitals. And while I am on the subject of educational grants, I would like to ask the government, and especially our great Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet, to find a way to increase these educational grants even though a small-time politician tries to frighten Canadians into letting him remain in power by telling them tall tales about the federal government's intention to encroach on provincial rights. The great majority of them know that there is no truth in this statement as they have shown by their vote in the 1949 election. Is there a single hon. member sitting for a federal constituency who is not as concerned with his province's rights as the hon. member who sits for the same constituency in the provincial legislature? One must be logical. I am as good a citizen of Ontario as my hon. friend who sits tor my constituency in the provincial legislature and the same holds true for every member of the house. But there is nothing new in such petty politics. It dates back to before 1911.
Every time the Liberals, in Ottawa, endeavoured to pass a social security measure, there was shouting about provincial autonomy. It was always a matter of playing a little game of local politics to ingratiate themselves with their constituents. Nobody that I know of returned a single cheque. I have never heard it said that the hon. member for Labelle, Mr. Short-Sight (Untranslatable pun on Courte-manche, "short sleeve"), I mean Mr. Courtemanche; I am sorry if I called him by that name but there are lots of people in the county of Labelle who call him that

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the budget sometimes take us far afield, but I intend to confine my remarks to certain of the more technical aspects of the budget itself.
I should like to make a plea for greater clearness and greater simplicity in the presentation of the budget. The five million Canadians who constitute the earning portion of our population have a very great interest in the budget for it informs them whether their incomes are going to be affected for better or for worse. The direct taxation imposed' by personal income taxes is of concern to<

three million people, and is perhaps the most interesting feature of the budget. It is on behalf of this great mass of taxpayers that I suggest that the budget should be presented in such a way that the taxpayer's obligation is clearly evident on the first reading.
For the business world in general there is perhaps no special need for any alteration in the form, because they have experts who can and do make analyses of the budget changes. But is there any reason why the changes in personal income taxes should not be set out with the greatest clearness? In earlier budgets finance ministers went to the trouble of giving precise examples of the changes contemplated, Mr. Ilsley did that with his budget in 1942, when the income tax proposals were combined with compulsory savings.
Contrast that candour with the situation this year. It may very well be said that the personal income tax changes were set out, but I submit that to the taxpayer the 2 per cent charge on his income for old age security, listed as a separate item on the income tax form, is part and parcel of his income tax. Changes in rates were announced and tables appeared in Hansard and in the budget papers showing the details, but the picture was not clear. Concealed in microscopic print was the information that in addition to the rates set out in the table the old age security tax of 2 per cent had to be applied.
Instead of setting out with the greatest clearness the actual amounts, inclusive of the old age security tax, that the income taxpayer will have to contribute, the budget simply sets out the tables and leaves the problem to the individual taxpayer or to the newspapers. Calculations of the old age security tax could have been set up in an adjoining column and the full picture would then have been available to the taxpayer.
There may have been no desire or attempt to mislead, but when due allowance was not made in the tables for the old age security tax, the information supplied was misleading. Also misleading was the emphasis placed on the 11 per cent decrease in the income tax. The actual reduction for the income taxpayer on his 1953 income is certainly no more than 54 per cent.
I am prepared to grant that in the minister's speech, in the table and in the fine microscopic notes all necessary information was available, but I do insist that no taxpayer should have to read the budget twice over to discover its meaning, or sharpen a pencil and make elaborate calculations. The information should be set out clearly. Simple things should be expressed simply.
Ministers of finance could take a lesson from municipal finance authorities. The prop-
The Budget-Mr. Churchill erty owner gets a clear and unambiguous statement as to his assessment and mill rate. No special effort, no detailed calculations are necessary. A similar clear statement could be made to the income taxpayer. There is plenty of scope in the budget for all manner of intricate financial statements and calculations. Economists, accountants, financial experts and ministers of finance may have the clearest knowledge of such terms as extrabudgetary transactions, unmatured funded debt, deferred credits and contingent liabilities, but millions now living will die overtaxed and underinformed about these matters.
I am sure that the average Canadian taxpayer is concerned very seriously in regard to his income tax. He understands very clearly what happens to his pocketbook when he makes his payment, but he tends to leave to others the intricacies of the financial problems involved. Terms should not be unnecessarily invented or distorted. One term is used which as far as I can find out first appeared in the budget speech of 1951. It has now by 1953 reached the status of being incorporated in the tables and in the public accounts. I refer to the term "non-budgetary". How you can have budgetary items and non-budgetary items in what is called a budget raises a problem in the use or misuse of language. The word "budget" is defined by the Oxford English dictionary as follows:
A statement of the probable revenue and expenditure for the ensuing year with financial proposals founded thereon.
Webster's dictionary gives a more detailed definition as follows:
A financial statement of the estimated revenues and expenditures of a country and, by extension, a plan or program for financing a government based on such a statement including authorization to collect the revenues and incur the expenses proposed.
Canadian practice during the last few years has tended to narrow the expression down to merely the revenues collected by taxation and the expenditure of those particular funds. But there are other sources of revenue besides taxation, and there are other uses of government funds besides departmental expenditures. These were formerly called loans, advances and investments. In my opinion that description should have been retained and the expression "non-budgetary" dropped. I suggest that some better description of these other accounts might be devised.
I notice another change of a more serious nature in this year's budget. It is a bookkeeping entry and does not affect materially the over-all picture, except to put things in a better light than the actual facts warrant. I refer to the so-called temporary loan of $100 million to the old age security fund

The Budget-Mr. Churchill shown on page 62 of the white paper under the general heading of non-budgetary disbursements and the subheading of loans, investments and working capital advances. This item appears again on page 69 of the table listing cash and other current assets as a departmental working capital advance. It is considered to be an active asset.
In the budget an asset may be either active or non-active. The distinction was first made about 35 years ago. I searched for a definition of "non-active", and I found it in the budget speech presented by Mr. Bennett in June, 1931, a speech which I think is a model of clarity and orderly arrangement. He defined non-active assets as being loans and advances made for various enterprises which are not presently realizable, yield no direct return to the treasury and in the presentation of the accounts are treated as losses. Examples occur at the bottom of page 2209 of the budget appendix this year. The converse would be true of active assets, and they were defined in the budget paper of 1949 on page 1858 as follows:
Essentially these consist of assets which yield interest, profits or dividends, together with very liquid assets such as cash and departmental working funds.
In the budget papers of this year that definition is watered down a bit to include the words "for the most part", and the definition reads as follows:
These, for the most part, consist of assets that yield interest, profits or dividends, very liquid assets such as cash and departmental working capital funds, and certain prepaid expenditures and sundry suspense accounts.
I do not see that the $100 million loan to the old age security fund is an active asset. It is not likely to be realized, and it yields no direct return to the treasury. It should be shown, in my opinion, as a non-active asset and therefore as an expenditure. It is called a temporary loan, a term usually employed for a three or six months' period. There is no prospect of this advance to the old age security fund being paid back, certainly not in the near future. The expenditures of the fund for the fiscal year now ending exceed receipts by $100 million. In the next fiscal year the estimated expenditures will exceed the estimated receipts by $67 million. Will we then have in the 1954 budget another $67 million listed as a temporary loan to the old age security fund and treated as an active asset?
Since confederation there have been 21 occasions on which the unmatured public debt has been reduced. On each of these occasions there was not only a cash surplus of ordinary revenue from taxation over

ordinary expenditure, but also a decrease in the net debt, which occurs when the net active assets increase and the gross debt is correspondingly decreased. But there have been occasions when ministers of finance have declared that the financial year has ended in a surplus when in actual fact no reduction in the unmatured public debt was made. This declaration of a surplus comes as the result of resorting to the expediency of listing among the active assets items that should more properly be called non-active and appear as expenditures.
Mr. Fielding, minister of finance in 1922, dealt at some length with this matter as reported in the Hansard of that period at page 2105. I should like to quote three or four sections from his budget speech in explanation of this matter. He said:
A finance minister who has the good fortune to produce a surplus . . . may find, and very often will find, that he meets with this criticism: Oh, you have no such surplus; you actually have run into debt during the year. The method in the past of showing a surplus has been to take what is called the ordinary expenditure of the country . . . and set against it the revenue of the year, which left you either a surplus or a deficit. If that revenue is more than the ordinary expenditure you will nave a surplus; if it is less than the ordinary expenditure you will have a deficit.
But every year there are expenditures which do not appear in that calculation. The objection made in times past was well founded. It was and is a fact that there are always expenditures of a special character, and the criticism that has been made in times past is in that respect correct. The distinction that is drawn between capital expenditure and ordinary expenditure has often been a subject of debate . . .
It is not an unfair claim to make if the facts be clearly understood. It has always been the method by which our public accounts have been conducted. So when the accounts for 1920-21 claimed that there was a large surplus of $73 million, the method of bookkeeping was being followed that had existed in the past, yet as a matter of fact during that year there was actually an increase in the public debt of $92 million and over, the difference, of course, representing the charges to capital and special account and that now ever-growing account, the railway service of the country.
Mr. Fielding then went on to give an account of his own fiscal year for which he was then reporting in these words:
The result of the operations for the year just closed-
The reference is to 1921-22.
-is that while we have according to one calculation a surplus, we have to acknowledge an addition to the public debt of $86,417,000.
Then Mr. Fielding proceeded to deal with the accounts which prior to his time had been causing this trouble in the budget presentation, and these accounts largely affected the railways. These are his words, as found at page 2106:
There may be an advantage and a convenience in separating the railway operations from the rest

of our expenditure. However, there is another view of the matter. We have a justification for charging to capital or to a special account some particular thing-the building of a railway, for instance. Various classes of public expenditure having permanent results may properly be classified as assets, may properly be classified under capital account. But if from year to year we are to provide for the ordinary expenses of the railway; if we are to provide for the deficit, the difference between receipts and expenditure; if we are also to provide large sums for interest on the bonds and other securities of these so-called railway companies-if we are to do that unfailingly every year ... it will be open to some to say, with much justice, that this is no longer a special account but part of the ordinary expenditure of the country; and if so, that ordinary expenditure should be included before we undertake to declare a surplus.
It seems to me that there is a great similarity between these railway advances to which Mr. Fielding referred and the loans made in recent years to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and certain working capital advances to departments, as for example to the Department of Agriculture for the agricultural prices support program, not to mention this $100 million loan to the old age security fund to which I have already referred.
A search of the budget statements for the last 23 years does not disclose a single instance of a loan appearing as an active asset, in so far as I could discover, unless it was made to a crown corporation or a body expected to produce revenue. There is no instance that I could find of a loan to a governmental department which is merely a spending department. The loan to the old age security fund can be repaid only by means of taxation, for what other source of income is available?
In the year 1953 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) appears to have reverted to the practice which Mr. Fielding condemned. He has a revenue surplus of $47-8 million, being the excess of tax revenue over departmental expenditures. He has increased the unmatured public debt by $141-7 million. By the expedient of calling the $100 million advance to the old age security fund an active asset, the gross debt has been reduced by $47-8 million and a surplus has been declared. Had the advance to the old age security fund been shown as an expenditure by the Department of National Health and Welfare or as a non-active asset and, therefore, as a loss, the so-called surplus would have been wiped out and a deficit declared of $52-2 million.
The Minister of Finance was able to reduce the unmatured public debt in each of the fiscal years from 1947 to 1952. In the fiscal year 1952-53 he has increased the unmatured public debt by $141-7 million. The year ends with a deficit, not a surplus.
The Budget-Mr. Churchill
Another feature of the budget which is open to criticism is that a complete picture of revenues and expenditures is not presented. At page 2135 of Hansard the minister stated that radio licence fees have never been treated as part of our tax revenue, nor are these receipts shown in the tables in the white paper. This stems, of course, from the desire to treat the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as a separate corporate body with a direct source of revenue. And the proposed 15 per cent special excise tax on radio and television sets, etc., may be treated in the same way as the former radio licence fee.
Similarly the old age security system has "relieved" the budget of $110 million, as the minister stated at page 2121 of Hansard. In the tables of revenue in the white paper the old age security receipts-being 2 per cent on personal income tax-corporation and sales tax are shown as deductions from the total receipts of these taxes but are not grouped together. In the expenditure table no item appears.
I am not offering objection to the setting up of a separate account or separate fund for old age security as approved in the fall of 1951 but we have now reached the point when the budget does not disclose all the revenue received. Yet the main source of revenue remains the same-taxation.
All revenue is required to be paid into the consolidated revenue fund. In the minutes of the proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on public accounts for December, 1951, the late Dr. Clark called this, and these are his words-
-a cardinal statutory requirement, namely the creation of a single consolidated revenue fund into which all public money is required to be deposited to the credit of the receiver general. This is the most important single principle on the revenue side, the greatest protection of the rights of parliament in the control of the public purse. This goes back to section 102 of the British North America Act.
In the Financial Administration Act public money is defined as:
(i)	duties and revenues of Canada
(ii)	money borrowed by Canada or received through the sale of securities
(iii)	money received or collected by or on behalf of Canada, and
(iv)	money paid to Canada for a special purpose.
That being the case, I would think that in the budget all receipts and disbursements of public money should be disclosed. Unless this is done, we will have for the future some such division as the following: (1) the budget proper being, in part but not entirely,

The Budget-Mr. Drew the receipts from taxation and the departmental expenditures of the same; (2) certain so-called non-budgetary items making up part of our active assets; (3) a separate account, not appearing in the budget, of receipts from taxation for the old age security fund; and (4) another separate account not appearing in the budget of receipts from taxation for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Will we have in future the presentation of the budget proper followed later by baby budgets for special funds or accounts?
In summary, I have been suggesting:
(1)	greater clearness and simplicity in the budget with particular reference to the personal income tax;
(2)	discontinuance of the use of the term "non-budgetary";
(3)	the listing of so-called loans to the old age security fund as expenditures;
(4)	a more careful distinction between active and non-active assets; and
(5)	a complete account in the budget of all public moneys received and expended.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken it is my intention to deal with the amendment to the amendment and explain our position in regard to that motion before the house upon which we will have the first vote.
This has been an extended debate, but there have been some encouraging demonstrations of the fact that arguments such as have been made have had their effect. To that extent the people of this country already have benefited very substantially by the discussion which has taken place. For instance, as the result of the statements made in this debate by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), the government changed its position in regard to the education tax in the province of Quebec, and that province has benefited by the decision announced in this house a few days ago. The fact that it comes eight years too late is not in any way to suggest that it is not satisfactory to see this very improper situation remedied as a result of discussions which have taken place. It is an argument in favour of this type of free discussion, which sometimes comes under criticism, when we see substantial results of this nature.
There is also the fact that, because of remarks in this debate about taxation which had been imposed on farmers, and which the deputy minister had carefully explained was imposed upon farmers, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) rose in the house and

gave an interpretation which was much more satisfactory.
We have had other examples of the same kind during this debate, and perhaps it may be very unfortunate that the debate is nearing an end, because who knows but that under constant pressure the government might make further adjustments that are in keeping with arguments made from this side of the house, not during this debate alone but for several years.
I am not going back over some of the things that have been said in this house, Mr. Speaker, and I will do no more in that respect than express the hope that those outside this house who do read Hansard will read a speech that was made here tonight, and will know that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was in his seat at the time, as well as several other ministers. The remarks which are on the record, and which I hope will be read, are an indication of some of the kinds of remarks made on the other side of the house which meet with approval of members on that side.
I need say no more because the remarks that were made speak eloquently for themselves. They are a preview of the kind of thing that doubtless some of us may expect in the coming election, whenever that may be. It is a challenge to the people of Canada to decide what they are going to do upon the basis of the facts presented to them, and not on the basis of any such presentation as that which appears on record in Hansard here tonight.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the amendment to the amendment must be taken in conjunction with the amendment itself and, therefore, I propose to read together the amendment and the subamendment because it is upon the two combined that the vote will be taken. The amendment reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that under the present budget the government proposes to take more money from the taxpayers of Canada than ever before for non-defence and defence expenditures without any effective steps being taken to:
(a) deal with waste, extravagance and administrative inefficiency; (b) give tax relief to those who need it most; (c) offer any encouragement to Canadian farmers in meeting the serious consequences of lost markets and lower prices resulting from the government's agricultural and marketing policies; (d) permit an independent inquiry into the organization accounting and administration of the Department of National Defence."
Then the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has moved that the following be added thereto:
This house further regrets that the present budget is a rich man's budget which:

(1)	makes tax cuts retroactive to January 1st for corporations but not for individual Canadians;
(2)	doubles the exemption levels for the full corporation tax rate while leaving exemption levels for individual Canadians unchanged; and
(3)	doubles the credits allowed to shareholders for dividends, but gives no comparable credits to those who do the work that produces the dividends.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, we support the subamendment which I have read, and I wish to indicate the words that are of importance in that subamendment. First there is the criticism that tax cuts are made retroactive to January 1 for corporations but not for individual Canadians. Some attempt has been made to interpret that as a criticism of these retroactive tax cuts to corporations. That is not what the paragraph says. What it says is that the criticism is directed to the making of the corporation tax cuts retroactive, and not making the reduction to individual Canadians retroactive to that date.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I do not know how any hon. member in this house can seriously argue that this is not a proper criticism. After all, if it is appropriate to make that reduction for corporations, as I think it is, it is certainly equally appropriate and more appropriate to make the reduction for individual taxpayers who are feeling the burden,. and who have had less opportunity to adjust themselves than the corporations.
Then, under paragraph (2) of the subamendment, we find these words:
-doubles the exemption levels for the full corporation tax rate while leaving exemption levels for individual Canadians unchanged;
Again, this does not say what has been attributed to it. It certainly does not, in the words, no matter what arguments may have been made, criticize the doubling of the exemption levels for the corporation tax. But it does criticize the government for making that adjustment without giving consideration to the further exemption of individual Canadian taxpayers. Certainly we do agree with that criticism. We believe there should have been an increase in the exemption to corporations, but we believe that the first place this exemption should have been increased was in the case of individual Canadian taxpayers. We have argued for that right along.
Then we come to the third paragraph in the subamendment and we find this:
-doubles the credits allowed to shareholders for dividends, but gives no comparable credits to those who do the work that produces the dividends.
Again we find that there is criticism of doubling the credits to those who receive their income from dividends on corporation securities, without any comparable credits to those who produce those dividends by their 68108-1872
Th<? Budget-Mr. Drew work. With that criticism we agree. We say that the first place consideration should have been given right along the line is to the individual taxpayer who is finding difficulty in meeting the tax burdens that he now faces.
There is, of course, one special feature related to this third paragraph which is extremely difficult to understand. Most certainly the Canadian taxpayer who feels the burden of taxes today, whose return from his work is not sufficient to allow him to adjust himself to the increasing burden, finds it extremely difficult to understand how the man or woman who is in the fortunate and rare position of having an income of up to $9,600 exclusively from dividends from corporation securities will not pay one cent of taxes. This is something that has not been in any way satisfactorily explained to the members of this house.
Believing as we do that there should be reductions, and that there could be very much greater reductions all along the line than are before us now, we certainly find it difficult to understand how one can explain to the hard-working man or woman who is earning $2,000, $3,000 or $3,500, why they must be called upon to pay the heavy taxes they do pay, while the person who receives close to $10,000 from corporation dividends pays not one cent in the form of income tax.
I hope no one is going to say, "But how much income tax does a person getting $2,000 pay"? That is, of course, the joker. The joker is that there has been no reduction whatever in any of the taxes that really bear most heavily on the worker and the person with a small income. The place where the taxes really pinch is in the case of a person on a small pension, with a small fixed income from savings which were accumulated during years of work in the hope that he had enough to live quietly, securely and comfortably for the rest of his life. These people now find their dollars worth less than 50 cents in terms of the dollars they put away. They cannot meet their obligations, but those people are paying heavy taxes.
Do not let anyone try to fool them. In spite of the statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that whatever might be done to fool the public no attempt should be made to fool the members here, we hope no attempt will be made by the government to fool the public in regard to these taxes. These people pay the 10 per cent sales tax on many of the things they need. They pay excise taxes on the things they must have. There have been no adjustments in these taxes, and yet these are the most inflationary taxes of

The Budget-Mr. Drew all. The excise tax is most inflationary, and the sales tax is next. Nothing has been done to adjust those, although our sales tax is at 10 per cent, and although our excise taxes are very high and hit the general public at many points.
We intend to vote for the subamendment. What is more, we hope that hon. members on the other side will read that subamendment carefully, as well as the amendment, and consider quite carefully exactly what it is they are doing if they vote both against that amendment and the subamendment. What they are doing is to express their approval of an adjustment of taxes which offers no relief at all to those with the smallest incomes, which offers very little relief to the worker with a relatively small income, and which offers no appreciable relief of any kind to the farmers of this country, but does offer substantial relief in the higher brackets in corporation taxes.
Once again let me point out that any suggestion that has come from the other side that support of this amendment or subamendment constitutes criticism of the reduction of these taxes is absolutely remote from reality, and I hope that is a sufficiently parliamentary expression to suggest a great deal more. They know perfectly well that we have been arguing in favour of the reductions for years. Last year we argued for them; a year ago we argued for them, and the year before that we argued for them; but we were given many reasons why it could not be done.
One of the advantages of democracy is that we have recurrent elections; and at least to the extent that anybody gets any consideration out of this budget they should express their thanks to the democratic processes which bring an election around from time to time and stir the conscience of the government periodically in this way. A few years ago we had cyclical budgeting. Now we have a cyclical conscience, and that conscience asserts itself. But it did not get a chance to assert itself quite far enough, and it did not assert itself in the very place where that conscience would have produced results most satisfactory to the people of this country.
Yes, we are going to support the subamendment which carries with it the amendment. In doing so we certainly regret that at no stage in the session has there been the slightest indication on the part of the government that it was prepared to recognize that there are things that could be done to lighten the burden of taxation on the people of Canada by reducing the amount which is going to be collected from the taxpayers

during the coming year. There have been, of course, those two satisfactory changes of heart, and we congratulate the government on those. We congratulate the government on the fact that it did respond to the demand of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and made an adjustment with regard to that extremely improper provision under which there was no exemption for the education tax levied in Quebec.

We welcome this. As a matter of fact, strange' though it may seem, we have persisted in the hope that more concessions might be made as a result of the arguments that have been put forward. But having made those concessions-and they certainly were not unimportant concessions; we agree that that is so

we now find that the government has apparently hardened its heart, closed the doors and is saying: Here it is; there is nothing more; we are not prepared to admit that anything further could be done.

I think it would be appropriate if some of the hon. members would just refresh their memories because, whatever might have been said on earlier occasions, it certainly is a surprising thing to hear the statement made on behalf of the government that there is no foundation for the suggestion that there is waste and extravagance.
There is not an hon. member in this house who does not recognize that in the wide ramifications of government today there are bound to be mistakes, and that duplicating services are bound to develop, with the very best of intentions. But also there is not an hon. member in this house who does not know that, when those things occur, prudence would suggest that steps be taken to make inquiries and find out how that situation can be dealt with. There is not a single business enterprise in this country that would not follow that course in attempting to save money by increasing the efficiency of the general operation, without thinking for one moment that they were dealing with the possibility of dishonesty or anything of that kind within their own corporate enterprise. But businesses in this country, whether they be corporate or private, which seek to keep themselves solvent and to make profits, recognize that in the very nature of things, as business expands, various details are not as efficient as they should be, and that therefore it is wise from time to time to conduct an examination and improve the methods by which that business is done. That is what we have been suggesting on different occasions. That is what we have suggested again during this session, and it is what has been suggested over and over again in the course of the arguments during this present debate.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk of no foundation for the suggestion of waste and extravagance, first of all let us remember that we have two reports before us. We have the report of the Auditor General which tells the members of this house that there are eight different systems of accounting in the Department of National Defence, and that nothing effective has been done to improve that situation. That is something about which we should be concerned; that is something we have drawn to the attention of the hon. members of the house; and that is something the government could have assured the members of the house would be dealt with before we passed this budget.
We know perfectly well that, with the presentation of the budget, it is not going to be possible to conduct an inquiry such as is needed with regard to any of these problems before the budget has been passed so
The Budget-Mr. Drew the ordinary business activities of government itself may be carried on. But if the government had given an undertaking that such an inquiry would be conducted and had actually instituted an inquiry of this nature, then the members of this house could have said to their constituents and to the people of Canada generally: As a result of the arguments that have been presented, as a result of the arguments that you have sent in to us, the government has taken steps to conduct the kind of inquiry which we hope will lead to the elimination of waste and extravagance which you know does exist. But that has not been done. On the contrary, whenever the suggestion is made it is laughed at; it is ridiculed and met with the statement that there is no foundation for the suggestion of waste and extravagance.
Every hon. member knows that a system is inefficient, with eight different kinds of accounting and in that way an absence of effective supervision. Then we had the Currie report. There we had the most fantastic waste and extravagance that has been exposed at any time. Let us all remember that the details are still there. A railway siding was stolen; and it must surely appeal to the imagination to have the suggestion that you can build a new railway siding for a few thousand dollars. When we hear the statements that are made as to what it will cost to replace that railway siding that was stolen, then one begins to wonder what kind of accounting system there is at any place in the Department of National Defence. I do not think any hon. member has any doubt as to how expensive it would be to replace that railway siding.
Then let us remember that the horses are still on the payroll, and they still demonstrate the administrative inefficiency to which we refer. Let us also remember that all these bags of cement were stolen, and all the equipment was stolen that was mentioned. The fact that some of it was recovered has not in any way disposed of the fact that here is positive evidence of waste and extravagance, and that we have no evidence before us that anything effective is being done to stop that kind of waste and extravagance elsewhere.

I am not prohibited by the rules of the house from referring to the sittings of that committee in other sessions, and that is what I am referring to. I would point out that this committee, set up with great hopes, has on every occasion used the majority supporting the government to prevent the kind of inquiry that all of us hoped would take place when it was set up. What will happen at this time, of course, I am not in a position to guess; but at any rate it would be a very encouraging change if there were any difference.
The point is it is not only before any committee but right in this house that requests have been made for other reports that we know exist, and of which extracts have been read into the record. Let the government deny that those extracts read into the record are not contained in the reports that were referred to. There is the report of Mr. Walter Gordon, another highly competent, reputable, experienced and respected chartered accountant. He also examined into certain aspects of the administration of government. We have

been asking for that report. That belongs to the people of Canada, not to this government. We as the representatives of the people of Canada have a right to see the report that was paid for by the money of the people of Canada, and which this government has no right to hold as its secret possession.
There are other reports which have been referred to and which the government has refused to produce, other reports paid for with the people's money, other reports which deal with the details of government administration. Those reports belong to the people of Canada, and I repeat that the members of this house who are the representatives of the people of Canada have a right to see what those reports contain. The government should have presented those reports to this house without any hesitation when they were asked for. I hope that within the course of this present debate-while I hope a vote on the amendment to the amendment may be taken tonight, it would seem that the vote on the main motion may not be tonight- the government will still let us see these reports which would be extremely helpful in discussing the subjects that are before the house for consideration.
Over and over again we have heard the suggestion that a certain level of taxation is the irreducible minimum. We are told that out of all taxes that are paid so much is for defence and so much for social security, and that these cannot be reduced. The evidence is clearly before us that expenses could be reduced without any reduction of efficiency. That applies to expenditures not only on defence but on other things as well.
