speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has been dealing with the request from the government for the largest sum of money ever asked for in a single year at any time in peace or war from the taxpayers of Canada. Do not let anyone be beguiled into the mistaken idea that there is a reduction in the amount of taxes to be taken from Canadian taxpayers this year. There is not. There is an increase in both defence and nondefence expenditures. That increase is going to come from the Canadian taxpayers. That increase is going to be paid in various ways. In the end it is going to be paid by the ordinary taxpayer across Canada, no matter where the incidence of that tax may be.
With respect to one of the points that have been raised in this debate, I wish to make it perfectly clear that in supporting the subamendment we do not subscribe to certain things that have been said about corporation taxes. We believe it is desirable that there be a reduction in all taxes, and that the first and most important place to reduce taxes is in the case of those with the smallest incomes. We believe that those whose incomes are too
[Mr. Sinclair.1

small even to be called upon to pay income tax at all should have received some consideration by way of a reduction in both the Sales tax and the excise tax. We believe that reduction should have been general. We say it can be general and that there can be substantial reductions right across the board; but we do not agree with the idea that, having improved the position of the small taxpayer, any advantage is going to be gained by the small taxpayer through piling taxes on the corporations.
There is one perfectly good reason for that statement which should be borne in mind. It is only natural that many people think of corporations as big operations from which money can be taken painlessly without the ordinary taxpayers feeling the pinch. Let us be realists. Everyone in this house knows that as corporation taxes go up, those taxes are added to the cost of the products for which the people of this country pay. The result is that high corporation taxes are and have been extremely inflationary, and have contributed substantially to the inflation that we have felt in this country. When the statement is made that inflation has been licked that is indeed a misconception of the situation. All that has happened is that the very great inflation that has taken place has been halted, but inflation has not been licked.
Ask the person who is getting a pension that he thought ten or fifteen years ago was going to be enough to take care of him, whether he thinks there is no inflation in the country. Ask people who put their money into endowment policies years ago, thinking they were providing enough for their old age, if inflation has been licked. They will tell you it has not. All that has happened is that inflation has been temporarily frozen. We believe that inflation should be tackled and really tackled, and we believe it can be tackled by reducing the expenditures of government. We believe that the effect on inflation will be more than merely a reduction of the amount that would have been wasted otherwise; we believe that the example offered by a real effort to reduce government expenditure will have its impact right down the line.
We have the statements of economists, of businessmen, yes, of bankers, who are in the habit of dealing with these things, that high taxes and uncontrolled government expenditure encourage reckless expenditure both by corporations and by individuals. Over and over again it has been stated by economists of high standing and repute that there is nothing which contributes more to anti-inflationary pressure than an example being offered by government itself of simply good 68108-188
The Budget-Mr. Drew business methods in tackling high expenditures. That is what we have been asking for over and over again.
What we do say is this. Let us have the most efficient and effective defence forces that we can possibly have. Let us make sure that when we are spending the colossal sum of over $2 billion for defence, for something that is not productive in the ordinary sense of industrial, agricultural or mining production, every one of these defence dollars is properly spent and that we get as close as possible to 100 cents on the dollar in value in spending that money. It would be a refreshing and encouraging thing if, instead of this resistance to any suggestions, the government would say quite frankly to members of the house; "We know that, when we get into such an unusual field of expenditure as defence expenditure in peacetime, it is almost impossible to keep the same effective check on spending as it is with respect to ordinary expenditure. We welcome any suggestions that come to us as to ways in which savings can be made. We will listen to your proposals, and we will act upon them wherever they will produce some satisfactory result." But, when we see smiles and laughter on the other side, let it not be suggested for one moment that something cannot be done to tackle this problem.
Again, let us remember that our system of government is a combination of the British and the American systems of government. We have the parliamentary system of Britain and the federal system of the United States; and there are many similarities to both in our own unique system. A few days ago, when it was suggested from this side that an inquiry be conducted to examine the whole organization of government, it was said by a member of the government on behalf of the government-

Well, Mr. Speaker, I will put it this way. The government has not been willing to agree that it would be desirable that there should be an inquiry into the organization and administration of government. Any suggestion that such a course might not be consistent with the practice at Westminster indicates that anyone who is making such a statement is not aware of what has actually taken place at Westminster; because the fact is that the present organization at Westminster was the result of an inquiry into the organization of government which produced very striking and very effective reforms. It is because that system proved so satisfactory at Westminster many years ago

The Budget-Mr. Drew that we have continued to press for an examination of that nature.
Let us see what has happened in the United States. They have had an inquiry there into the organization of certain of their defence administration. The commission that was appointed, as experts, believe they can save 10 per cent of their defence expenditures with an actual improvement in the quality and the effectiveness of the weapons, of the equipment and of the defence forces themselves.
It is not, of course, possible to say that because 10 per cent was the figure found by a highly competent commission in the United States, we would necessarily get the same result here. But it is possible to say that in a government administering a system very similar in many ways to theirs, it would be just a little more than human if some savings could not be discovered at some point by an inquiry of this nature.
Let me point out something else that has been done by the government of the United States. That government have many problems similar to ours because of the fact that they also are on the North American continent. As we are, they are called upon to make certain expenditures overseas for military establishments of various kinds. The committee of Congress that was appointed for the purpose of conducting that inquiry has just reported that immense sums could be saved by applying ordinary business methods to the supervision of expenditures on these overseas establishments, necessary because of the fact that our forces are overseas. We have that report and we have the report of the Sarnoff commission in regard to the military organization. We now know that there is an inquiry being conducted by what President Eisenhower described as "a task force of one hundred experts" into the organization of government.
These are things that are being done by a government situated on the same continent, also with a federal system and also with overseas commitments similar in many ways to our own. While we do not suggest for one

moment that we should imitate anyone else, let us be ready to admit that we have adopted many of our business practices from the United States. We have found many of their systems of accounting suitable to our needs, and we do believe that in those cases we can and will gain some advantage from seeing what they have done.
It is not long since we learned that Canada has spent $129 million on the Korean war. That is a lot of money; $129 million is a tremendous sum of money but, Mr. Speaker, $129 million is only a very small fraction of the $4 billion that we have spent since the beginning of the Korean period. Hon. members of this house have a duty, as well as a right, to find out where that remaining $3,800 million odd has gone and what results it has produced.
These are grave and serious hours. The news that comes to us from Europe today removes any suggestion that we are in a comfortable period where there are no great dangers in front of us. The events of yesterday and today, the cold-blooded murder of British airmen and the interference with the flight of a civilian aircraft going into Berlin, indicate the extent of the danger which is there all the time.
